# BoxyTrucks

> An enthusiast guide to boxy, body-on-frame 4x4s for hands-on owners: history, buying checks, DIY repairs with parts, service baselines, wheel and tire fitment, recalls, values and mods, one guide per generation. Facts are sourced on each page.

Fluid specs, capacities and torque figures are general guidance: always verify against the factory manual for the exact vehicle (see https://boxytrucks.com/about/disclaimer/). Parts links may be affiliate links.

Full text of every model guide: https://boxytrucks.com/llms-full.txt

## Toyota 4Runner

- [Toyota 4Runner overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/): Toyota's mid-size body-on-frame survivor — forty years of refusing to become a crossover while everything around it did.
- [Toyota 4Runner 1st Gen (1984–1989)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/1st-gen/): A Hilux pickup with a removable fibreglass lid — solid front axle until the 1986 switch to independent front suspension.
- [Toyota 4Runner 2nd Gen (1990–1995)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/2nd-gen/): Still Hilux underneath, but with a one-piece steel body and a coil-sprung four-link rear axle.
- [Toyota 4Runner 3rd Gen (1996–2002)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/3rd-gen/): The one that left the pickup behind: Prado-shared chassis, coils all round, optional rear E-locker — the cult classic.
- [Toyota 4Runner 4th Gen (2003–2009)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/4th-gen/): Prado 120-based and bigger, with the only V8 4Runner (the 2UZ-FE) and X-REAS suspension on some trims.
- [Toyota 4Runner 5th Gen (2010–2024)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/5th-gen/): Fifteen model years on the J150 Prado/GX/FJ Cruiser platform with the 4.0 V6 — TRD Pro from 2015.
- [Toyota 4Runner 6th Gen (2025–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/6th-gen/): Moves to the TNGA-F (GA-F) frame shared with the Tacoma; turbo 2.4 four or the i-FORCE MAX hybrid, eight-speed auto.

## Chevrolet K5 Blazer & Suburban

- [Chevrolet K5 Blazer & Suburban overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/): General Motors took a half-ton pickup, cut a bit off the back and made the roof optional, and the Bronco and Scout never quite recovered. Then it did the opposite with the Suburban, giving it nine seats and four doors. Neither one is subtle, and both are easy to keep running.
- [Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1st generation) (1969–1972)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer-1st/): The original full-size Bronco fighter: a shortened K10 pickup with a lift-off top, 250 six or 307/350 V8, and front discs from 1971.
- [Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1973–1991) (1973–1991)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer/): The square body: a half-cab from 1976 with a removable rear top, small-block V8s, the 6.2 diesel and the M1009 Army Blazer.
- [Chevrolet/GMC Suburban (1973–1991 square body) (1973–1991)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/suburban-square/): The four-door, nine-seat truck wagon: 350 or 6.2 diesel, NP203/205/208 4x4, still a favorite tow rig and family overlander.

## Dodge Ramcharger

- [Dodge Ramcharger overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/ramcharger/): Dodge's answer to the Blazer and the Bronco was a half-ton Dodge pickup with the bed roofed over. It's big, thirsty and easy to underestimate, and today it sells for a lot less than a K5 Blazer.
- [Dodge Ramcharger (first generation) (1974–1980)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/ramcharger/ramcharger-1st/): The original: a shortened D-series 4x4 with a removable top, full-time 4WD until 1979 and V8s up to the 440, also sold as the Plymouth Trail Duster.
- [Dodge Ramcharger (1981–1993) (1981–1993)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/ramcharger/ramcharger-2nd/): The fixed-roof Ram-based truck: part-time 4WD, the CAD front axle from 1985, fuel injection from 1988 and Magnum V8s in 1992–93.

## Ford Bronco

- [Ford Bronco overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/): Ford's first SUV started as a 92-inch tin box with flat glass and a Dana 20, grew into an F-Series with a lift-off roof, vanished for 25 years and came back to fight the Jeep again. The first one is still the one everybody wants.
- [Ford Bronco (1966–1977) (1966–1977)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/early-bronco/): The original: a 92-inch-wheelbase roadster, half-cab or wagon with coil-sprung Dana 30/44 front, Ford 9-inch rear, Dana 20 and a six or a 289/302 V8.
- [Ford Full-size Bronco (1978–1996)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/full-size/): A short-wheelbase F-Series with a lift-off rear top: solid Dana 44 front axle and 351M/400 V8s in 1978–79, then Twin Traction Beam with the 300 six, 302 and 351W through 1996.
- [Ford Bronco II (1984–1990)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/bronco-ii/): The Ranger-based compact two-door on a 94-inch wheelbase: TTB front with a Dana 28 (Dana 35 from late 1989), Ford 7.5 rear, 2.8 then 2.9 Cologne V6, 2WD from 1986–87, and the rollover record that shaped the Explorer.
- [Ford Bronco (sixth generation) (2021–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/sixth-gen/): The revival on Ford's T6 frame: independent front suspension, solid rear axle, 2.3 and 2.7 EcoBoost, a seven-speed manual, the 35-inch Sasquatch package and the 37-inch Bronco Raptor.

## Mercedes-Benz G-Class

- [Mercedes-Benz G-Class overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/): A military box that became the world’s most expensive school-run accessory. Still devastating off-road — which most owners will never find out.
- [Mercedes-Benz G-Class W460 (1979–1991)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w460/): The original military-derived G, in short and long wheelbase, petrol and diesel.
- [Mercedes-Benz G-Class W461 (1992–2022)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w461/): The no-frills working G for militaries and professionals, kept alongside the luxury W463.
- [Mercedes-Benz G-Class W463 (1990–2018)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w463/): The civilian G: full-time 4WD, three lockers, ever-more luxury — and still solid axles.
- [Mercedes-Benz 500 GE V8 (1993–1994)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/500ge/): The limited-run first V8 G: 446 built, almost all in Amethyst Blue, with no front locker.
- [Mercedes-Benz Europa International Gs (1990s–2001)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/europa/): Federalized, US-VIN trucks imported by Europa of Santa Fe before Mercedes sold the G in America.
- [Mercedes-Benz G 500 (1998–2008)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g500/): The first regular-production V8 G and the first sold by Mercedes in the US.
- [Mercedes-Benz G 55 AMG (1999–2012)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g55-amg/): The hand-built AMG V8 version — the G that taught the world Gs could be fast.
- [Mercedes-Benz G 550 (2009–2018 (US))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g550/): The G 500 renamed for the US, with a 5.5-litre V8 and seven-speed automatic.
- [Mercedes-Benz G 63 AMG (2012–2018 (US 2013–2018))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g63-amg/): The biturbo AMG W463: 544–571 PS, seven speeds, and still three lockers on solid axles.
- [Mercedes-Benz G 63 AMG 6×6 (2013–2015)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g63-6x6/): An Australian Army six-wheeler with the AMG V8, five lockers and tyre inflation from the cab; about 100 built.
- [Mercedes-Benz G 500 4×4² (2015–2018)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/4x4-squared/): Portal axles, enormous ground clearance and absolutely no subtlety.
- [Mercedes-Benz G-Class (second generation) (2018–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/second-gen/): Independent front suspension, a modern cabin and still three locking differentials.

## Ineos Grenadier

- [Ineos Grenadier overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/grenadier/): A billionaire couldn't buy the old Defender, so he built his own from a pub table, a BMW engine and a pair of tractor axles. It is gloriously square, genuinely capable and steers like a canal boat (until 2026).
- [Ineos Grenadier Station Wagon (2022–present (US: 2024–present))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/grenadier/station-wagon/): The five-door, five-seat original: ladder frame, Carraro beam axles, BMW six, three lockable diffs available. US gets the petrol B58 only.
- [Ineos Grenadier Quartermaster (2023–present (US: 2025–present))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/grenadier/quartermaster/): Double-cab pickup on a 305 mm longer wheelbase, with a Euro-pallet-sized bed and up to 760 kg payload.

## AM General Hummer

- [AM General Hummer overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/): An Army truck with carpets, built on the same line as the real thing and twice as wide as common sense. It goes almost anywhere, seats four, and asks for an idler arm in return.
- [AM General Hummer H1 (1992–2006)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/h1/): The civilian HMMWV: portal hubs, inboard brakes, CTIS and GM diesels, ending with the 2006 Duramax Alpha.
- [AM General Hummer H2 (2003–2009)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/h2/): GM's Suburban-framed Hummer built by AM General: full-time 4WD, a standard rear locker and 35s from the factory, then a 6.2 and six-speed for 2008–09.

## International Scout

- [International Scout overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/): A tractor company's answer to the Jeep that accidentally invented the American SUV. Rusts like it's paid to, and owners forgive it every single time.
- [International Scout 80 / 800 (1961–1971)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-80-800/): The original Jeep fighter: four-cylinder Scout 80, then the more civilized 800 series with sixes and V8s.
- [International Scout II (1971–1980)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-ii/): The definitive Scout: IH V8s, Dana 44s, the 118-inch Traveler and Terra, a Nissan diesel and the Baja-winning SSII.
- [International Scout Motors Traveler & Terra (Announced 2022 · revealed 2024)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-motors/): Volkswagen Group's revival of the name, with a Traveler SUV and Terra pickup revealed in October 2024.

## Isuzu Trooper

- [Isuzu Trooper overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/): Isuzu drew a box, sold it under about a dozen badges on four continents, then spent four years in court defending its honour. The first one is a tall, honest tool; the second is a roomy V6 cruiser with a solid rear axle and a thirst for oil.
- [Isuzu Trooper (first generation) (1981–1991)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/trooper-1/): The original upright box: a pickup-based wagon with four-cylinder engines (and a late GM V6), sold in the US as the Trooper II.
- [Isuzu Trooper (second generation) (1991–2002)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/trooper-2/): Bigger and plusher, with Isuzu's 3.2 and 3.5 V6s, the Consumer Reports rollover fight and the Acura SLX twin.

## Jeep

- [Jeep overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/): The Jeep is the boxy 4x4 everyone else gets compared to, even the ones that got there first. It leaks, rattles and rusts, and it keeps selling, mostly to people who have already owned three.
- [Jeep CJ-5 (1955–1983)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-5/): Derived from the M38A1 military Jeep. Rounded door cutouts, Kaiser then AMC power, and 603,303 built across 29 years.
- [Jeep CJ-7 (1976–1986)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-7/): The CJ-5's 10-inch-longer, square-door evolution: room for an automatic, optional hardtop and steel doors, and AMC's 258 six. Nearly 380,000 were built.
- [Jeep CJ-8 Scrambler (1981–1986)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-8/): A CJ-7 stretched to a 103.5-inch wheelbase, with a removable half cab and a small pickup bed. Ronald Reagan kept one at his ranch.
- [Jeep Wagoneer & Cherokee (SJ) (1963–1983)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/sj-wagoneer/): The original 1963 Wagoneer and its 1974 two-door Cherokee spin-off: Quadra-Trac, AMC sixes and V8s up to the 401, and the wide-track Chief.
- [Jeep Grand Wagoneer (SJ) (1984–1991)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-wagoneer/): The full-size SJ wagon that began as the 1963 Wagoneer, renamed Grand Wagoneer for its final luxury-V8 years.
- [Jeep Cherokee XJ (1984–2001)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cherokee-xj/): The compact unibody Cherokee, with the 4.0-liter straight six from 1987. It was the template for the modern SUV.
- [Jeep Comanche MJ (1986–1992)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/comanche-mj/): The Cherokee XJ turned into a compact pickup: XJ unibody up front, a fully boxed frame behind the cab, two bed lengths and the 4.0 six from 1987. 190,446 were built.
- [Jeep Wrangler YJ (1987–1995)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/yj/): The first Wrangler, with square headlights and leaf springs. Track bars and anti-roll bars made it more civil than the CJ.
- [Jeep Grand Cherokee ZJ (1993–1998)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-cherokee-zj/): The first Grand Cherokee: coil-sprung solid axles, a 4.0 six or Magnum V8, Quadra-Trac and the one-year 5.9 Limited. Now one of the cheapest coil-sprung solid-axle 4x4s to buy.
- [Jeep Wrangler TJ (1997–2006)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj/): Coil springs and round headlights return on the short wheelbase. Many people think it's the best-riding classic Wrangler.
- [Jeep Wrangler Unlimited (LJ) (2004–2006)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj-unlimited/): The long-wheelbase TJ: more cargo room, a calmer ride and a short production run.
- [Jeep Wrangler JK (2-door) (2007–2018)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk/): A bigger, wider and more refined two-door Wrangler. In the US it had V6 power: a 3.8 at first, then the 3.6-liter Pentastar from 2012.
- [Jeep Wrangler JK Unlimited (2007–2018)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk-unlimited/): The first four-door Wrangler, and the one that took Jeep from niche toy to family car.
- [Jeep Wrangler JL (2018–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jl/): The current two-door Wrangler, more modern inside and out, refreshed for 2024.
- [Jeep Wrangler JL Unlimited (2018–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jl-unlimited/): The four-door JL, including the 4xe plug-in hybrid and the V8 Rubicon 392.
- [Jeep Gladiator JT (2020–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/gladiator-jt/): A JL Unlimited with a 137.3-inch wheelbase and a five-foot bed: Jeep's first pickup since the Comanche, with a 3.6 V6 or, for 2021–23, the 3.0 EcoDiesel. Refreshed for 2024.
- [Jeep Wagoneer & Grand Wagoneer (WS) (2022–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/wagoneer-ws/): The big names return on a body-on-frame, fully independent three-row SUV: Hemi V8s, then the Hurricane twin-turbo six, and a Wagoneer brand folded back into Jeep for the 2026 model year.

## Lada Niva

- [Lada Niva overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/niva/): A Zhiguli engine, Range Rover-style full-time 4WD and a body the size of a hatchback. It went to Antarctica, the North Pole and Everest base camp, and it's still in production nearly fifty years later.
- [Lada Niva (VAZ-2121 / 4x4 Legend) (1977–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/niva/niva/): The Soviet Union's unibody, full-time-4WD answer to the Land Rover: in production since 5 April 1977, and imported to the US under the 25-year rule.

## Toyota Land Cruiser

- [Toyota Land Cruiser overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/): The truck the rest of the world actually depends on — the one that turns up, fully loaded, in places where a breakdown isn't an inconvenience but a plot twist. Seven decades in, Toyota still hasn't figured out how to make it fragile.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser J20 / J25 (FJ25) (1955–1960)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj25/): The first Land Cruiser built for export and the first sold in America (one FJ25 in 1958): F 3.9 six, four-speed, single-speed transfer case and drums all round.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser FJ40 (1960–1984)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj40/): The two-door, short-wheelbase icon on leaf springs and F/2F straight-sixes — the truck that made the Land Cruiser name in America.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser FJ45 / FJ55 (1960–1984 (FJ45) · 1967–1980 (FJ55))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj45-fj55/): The long-wheelbase 40 Series pickups and wagons, and the FJ55 'Iron Pig' — Toyota's first Land Cruiser designed from the start as a wagon.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser FJ60 (1980–1987)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj60/): The square-rigged 60 Series wagon in its original form: carbureted 2F six, manual gearboxes, round headlights and leaf springs all round.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser FJ62 (1988–1990)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj62/): The 60 grows up: fuel-injected 3F-E, automatic gearbox, square headlights and the first push upmarket.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser 70 Series (1984–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/70-series/): The heavy-duty workhorse — wagons, troop carriers and pickups — still built for Africa, Australia, Latin America and the Middle East, and back on sale in Japan since 2023.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser 80 Series (1990–1997)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/80-series/): Coil springs, full-time 4WD, solid axles at both ends and optional triple lockers — for many owners, the last 'real' Land Cruiser.
- [Toyota Mega Cruiser (1995–2001)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/mega-cruiser/): Toyota's Humvee: the civilian version of the JGSDF Kōkidōsha, with hub-reduction drive, four-wheel steering and three locking diffs. Only 133 civilian trucks were registered in Japan.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 90 (1996–2002)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-90/): The mid-size Land Cruiser America never got: 3rd-gen 4Runner chassis, full-time 4WD, and 1KZ-TE or 1KD-FTV diesels. Now arriving as 25-year imports.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser 100 Series (1998–2007)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/100-series/): The big wagon goes upmarket: V8 power (and, for the US, independent front suspension) and the basis for the Lexus LX 470.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 120 (2002–2009)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-120/): The Lexus GX 470's non-V8 twin: Torsen center diff, 1GR-FE V6 or 1KD-FTV diesel (mind the injector seats). Not US-legal until the first trucks turn 25 in late 2027.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser 200 Series (2007–2021)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/200-series/): The V8 flagship and the last full-size Land Cruiser wagon sold in North America before Toyota pulled it after 2021.
- [Toyota FJ Cruiser (2007–2014 (US) · to 2022 elsewhere)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj-cruiser/): The retro FJ40 tribute on a Prado-family frame: 4.0 V6, a six-speed manual with full-time 4WD or an automatic with part-time 4WD, and a factory rear locker. Sold in the US for 2007–2014 and built for other markets until 2022.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 150 (2009–2023)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-150/): The fourth-generation Prado on the F2 ladder frame shared with the GX 460, 5th-gen 4Runner and FJ Cruiser: 1KD-FTV then 1GD-FTV diesels, a Torsen locking centre diff, KDSS, and a long DPF saga. Never sold in the US except as the Lexus GX 460.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser 250 Series (2024–present (US))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/250-series/): The Prado-based 'light-duty' Land Cruiser that brought the name back to the US: TNGA-F platform, 326-hp i-FORCE MAX hybrid, full-time 4WD with center and rear lockers standard.
- [Toyota Land Cruiser 300 Series (2021–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/300-series/): The current global flagship, unveiled in June 2021 — and not sold in the US or Canada.

## Land Rover Series & Defender

- [Land Rover Series & Defender overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/): The original farm-gate-to-Sahara tool: slow, leaky, drafty, and still the shape every other boxy 4x4 gets measured against.
- [Land Rover Series I–III (1948–1985)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/series/): Leaf springs, aluminium panels, selectable 4WD: the agricultural original that put the world's backcountry on wheels.
- [Land Rover 90 / 110 / Defender (1983–2016)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/defender-90-110/): Coil springs and permanent 4WD from the Range Rover under a Series-shaped body; named Defender from 1990, built until January 2016.
- [Land Rover Defender (L663) (2020–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/defender-l663/): The reboot: aluminium monocoque and independent suspension, unveiled September 2019 and launched as a 2020 model, officially sold in the US again.
- [Land Rover Discovery Series I (1989–1998)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-1/): Range Rover Classic chassis, suspension and 4WD under a cheaper family body; sold in the US from the 1994 model year.
- [Land Rover Discovery Series II (1998–2004)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-2/): The last Discovery on a ladder frame with live axles: Discovery 1 bones, P38 V8 and running gear, and a stack of electronics (ACE, SLS, HDC). Sold in the US for 1999–2004 as V8 automatics only.
- [Land Rover LR3 / Discovery 3 (2004–2009 (US: 2005–2009))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr3/): Ford-era clean sheet: Integrated Body Frame, four-corner air suspension and Terrain Response; V8 or V6 petrol as the LR3 in North America, TDV6 diesel elsewhere.
- [Land Rover LR4 / Discovery 4 (2009–2016 (US: 2010–2016))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr4/): Discovery 3 reworked with new engines and cabin: the last Discovery with a separate frame, cross-linked air suspension and Terrain Response; sold as the LR4 in North America.

## Lexus LX & GX

- [Lexus LX & GX overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/): Land Cruisers that went to finishing school and somehow kept their boots on. The badge says country club; the frame rails say Gobi Desert.
- [Lexus LX 450 (1996–1997)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx450/): The first Lexus truck, a lightly disguised 80 Series Land Cruiser with a 212-hp 4.5-liter straight-six. Sold for two US model years only.
- [Lexus LX 470 (1998–2007)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx470/): 100 Series Land Cruiser underneath, with the 4.7-liter 2UZ-FE V8 and hydraulic Adjustable Height Control (AHC) suspension.
- [Lexus LX 570 (2008–2021)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx570/): The 200 Series twin, powered by the 5.7-liter 3UR-FE V8 (383 hp in US/Canada trim).
- [Lexus LX 600 (2022–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx600/): Unveiled in October 2021 on the 300 Series platform. Swaps the V8 for a 409-hp 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6.
- [Lexus GX 470 (2003–2009)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx470/): Prado 120 underneath, with the 2UZ-FE V8 and a full-time 4WD system that has a locking center diff. Today it's one of the best-value overland platforms money can buy.
- [Lexus GX 460 (2010–2023)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx460/): Prado 150-based, with a 301-hp 4.6-liter V8, six-speed automatic and Torsen center locking differential. It famously earned (and lost) a Consumer Reports 'Don't Buy' in 2010.
- [Lexus GX 550 (2024–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx550/): Boxy again, and proud of it. It shares the GA-F platform with the Land Cruiser 250 and uses a 349-hp 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6.

## Mercedes-Benz Unimog

- [Mercedes-Benz Unimog overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/unimog/): A farm tractor that joined the army and never came home. Portal axles, locking diffs and a frame that twists like a pretzel make it close to unstoppable. It isn't quick, quiet or cheap to fix, and nobody who owns one cares.
- [Mercedes-Benz Unimog 404 (1955–1980)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/unimog/unimog-404/): The petrol-powered 1.5-tonne army Unimog S. Gaggenau built 64,242, the most of any Unimog series.
- [Mercedes-Benz Unimog U1300L (435) (1975–1993)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/unimog/unimog-u1300l/): The heavy-series diesel 4x4 that served as the Bundeswehr's 2-tonne truck and is now the classic expedition-camper base.

## Mitsubishi Delica

- [Mitsubishi Delica overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/delica/): Mitsubishi put a Pajero's low range under a minibus and called it a Delica. The result is the most improbable off-roader Japan ever exported by the shipload: slow, tall, right-hand drive and adored from British Columbia to the Dakar start line.
- [Mitsubishi Delica Star Wagon (L300 4WD) (1986–1999)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/delica/delica-l300/): The cab-over original: 4D56 turbo-diesel under the seats, part-time 4WD with low range, and Chamonix and Jasper specials.
- [Mitsubishi Delica Space Gear (1994–2007)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/delica/delica-space-gear/): A short hood, Super Select 4WD and Pajero engines, including the 2.8 4M40 diesel and 3.0 V6. More comfort and power for family camping.

## Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero

- [Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/): The Japanese 4x4 that went to the Sahara to prove it wasn't soft, then won the Dakar more times than any other car. It wore three names on three continents, and plenty of Land Cruiser owners learned to dislike all of them.
- [Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (First Generation) (1982–1991)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen1/): The original: torsion-bar IFS, part-time 4WD, 2.6 four, 3.0 V6 and Astron turbo-diesels, and the truck that won Paris–Dakar in 1985.
- [Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (Second Generation) (1991–1999)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen2/): Super Select 4WD, 6G72 and 6G74 V6s, 4D56 and 4M40 diesels, an optional rear locker and the Dakar-bred Pajero Evolution.
- [Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (Third Generation) (1999–2006)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen3/): Monocoque with a built-in frame, four-wheel independent suspension, Super Select 4WD II, 3.5/3.8 V6s and the 3.2 DI-D; US Montero 2001–2006, and the base for Mitsubishi's 2001–2005 Dakar wins.

## Nissan Patrol

- [Nissan Patrol overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/): The Land Cruiser's oldest sparring partner, and the one Americans mostly know from imported photos of the Outback. The coil-sprung GQ and GU are the reason Australians still argue about which Japanese wagon is tougher.
- [Nissan Patrol 60 Series (1960–1980)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/patrol-60/): The P-series 4.0 six, a three-speed and leaf springs; the only Nissan-badged vehicle sold in the US (1962–1969), now rare there and mostly re-imported from Colombia.
- [Nissan Patrol 160 / MQ (1980–1989)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/160-mq/): The last leaf-sprung Patrol: SD33, SD33T, L28 and P40 sixes, 24-volt MQ diesels, and the 1983 MK update with rectangular lights, a five-speed and the turbo-diesel.
- [Nissan Patrol Y60 (GQ) (1987–1997)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y60/): The first coil-sprung Patrol: solid axles at both ends, TB42, TD42 and RD28T sixes, and a Ford Maverick twin in Australia.
- [Nissan Patrol Y61 (GU) (1997–2016 (later in some markets))](https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y61/): The GQ's heavier, wider successor on the same solid-axle layout: TB48 and TD42T heroes, the ZD30's troubles, and utes and cab-chassis that outlived the wagon.
- [Nissan Patrol Y62 / Armada (2010–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y62/): The first independent-suspension, V8 Patrol: VK56VD, Hydraulic Body Motion Control, a Gulf best-seller, and sold in the US as the 2017–2024 Armada without the locker or HBMC.

## Steyr-Puch Pinzgauer

- [Steyr-Puch Pinzgauer overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/pinzgauer/): An Austrian army truck with an air-cooled engine, a backbone tube where the chassis should be and portal hubs at every corner. It is slow, loud and narrow, and it will follow a mountain goat up a hill.
- [Steyr-Puch Pinzgauer 710 / 712 (1971–1985)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/pinzgauer/pinzgauer-710-712/): The air-cooled petrol originals in 4x4 (710) and 6x6 (712) form. Nearly all US trucks are ex-Swiss Army.
- [Steyr-Puch Pinzgauer 716 / 718 (1985–2007)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/pinzgauer/pinzgauer-716-718/): The Turbo D: a VW turbodiesel six, disc brakes, a wider track and an optional automatic. Built in Graz until 2000, then in Britain.

## Land Rover Range Rover

- [Land Rover Range Rover overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/): The truck that taught a farm tool to wear a suit — and, for its first quarter-century, never forgot where it parked its wellies.
- [Land Rover Range Rover Classic (1970–1996)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/classic/): The original: two-door then four-door, coil springs, Rover V8, and a 24-year run that created the luxury 4x4.
- [Land Rover Range Rover P38A (1994–2002)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/p38/): Last of the ladder-frame, live-axle Range Rovers — 4.0/4.6 Rover V8s, standard air suspension and a lot more electronics.
- [Land Rover Range Rover L322 (2002–2012)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l322/): Monocoque body and all-independent air suspension; BMW-era engines at launch, Ford-era engines from 2005.
- [Land Rover Range Rover L405 (2012–2021)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l405/): All-aluminium monocoque that shed more than 400 kg versus the steel L322.
- [Land Rover Range Rover L460 (2022–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l460/): Fifth generation, revealed October 2021: seven-seat option, plug-in hybrids and a BMW-sourced 4.4 V8.

## Suzuki Samurai & Jimny

- [Suzuki Samurai & Jimny overview](https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/): The smallest proper 4x4 you can buy: ladder frame, two solid axles, low range and almost nothing else. It has been out-climbing trucks three times its size for more than half a century.
- [Suzuki Jimny LJ series (1970–1981)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/lj-series/): The original Jimny, a kei-class 4x4 that grew from a 359 cc air-cooled two-stroke to the 797 cc four-stroke LJ80.
- [Suzuki SJ / Samurai (1981–1998)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/samurai/): Leaf springs, a 1.3-litre G13 four and a 2,000-lb curb weight: the cult rock crawler that survived Consumer Reports.
- [Suzuki Jimny JB23 / JB43 (1998–2018)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/jimny-jb23/): Twenty-year, coil-sprung, ladder-frame Jimny; 1998–2001 trucks are now 25-year legal to import to the US.
- [Suzuki Jimny JB74 / JB64 (2018–present)](https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/jimny-jb74/): The retro-styled global cult hit with the 1.5 K15B and a 5-door from 2023; not US-importable until 2043.

## Quick answers: best years and biggest tires

- Toyota 4Runner 1st Gen, best years and years to avoid: 1984 and 1985. Toyota switched to independent front suspension with a three-inch-wider track for 1986, so 1986–89 trucks are IFS. Solid-axle trucks are the off-roader's favourite; IFS trucks ride better on the road. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/1st-gen/years/)
- Toyota 4Runner 1st Gen, biggest tire: Owners' consensus is 31x10.50R15 — Toyota-4Runner.org members say 31s fit with no lift and you can get away without regearing. 33x12.50s on a stock truck rub the front valance, wheel-well corners and rear pinch weld; IH8MUD owners estimate about 1.5 in of lift (plus some trimming) for 33s, and say the 22R-E will want lower gears. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/1st-gen/tires/)
- Toyota 4Runner 2nd Gen, best years and years to avoid: No year is a consensus pick, so buy the truck, not the date. Toyota's own V06 campaign paperwork says the 3VZ-E head-gasket failures were primarily limited to trucks built from January 1990 to October 1994, so a V6 built after that — or one with receipts for the gasket job — is the safer bet, and the 22R-E four sidesteps the issue entirely. Autotrader names no best year either, noting only that 1994 added side-impact door beams. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/2nd-gen/years/)
- Toyota 4Runner 2nd Gen, biggest tire: 31s — IH8MUD members call 31s the right size for a stock 2nd gen, and Toyota-4Runner.org owners agree 31x10.50R15 fits without a lift or regear. A narrow 33x10.50R15 can be squeezed in with some pounding and trimming, but expect rubbing at the valance and pinch weld; about 1.5 in of lift is the usual recommendation for 33s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/2nd-gen/tires/)
- Toyota 4Runner 3rd Gen, best years and years to avoid: IH8MUD's 3rd-gen regulars come closest to a consensus: 1999–2000 for a driver, ideally a Limited, and a '99 with the E-locker is the one most often called best (members say its springs sit about an inch longer than the '98 and 2000). 1996–98 trucks are cheaper and make good trail rigs. 2001–02 lose the locker for VSC and traction control, and one member flags occasional automatic planetary-gear problems. Rust and the lower ball joints matter more than any model year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/3rd-gen/years/)
- Toyota 4Runner 3rd Gen, biggest tire: The Toyota-4Runner.org consensus is 265/75R16 (roughly a 31.6-inch tire) on stock suspension. Some owners see rubbing at full compression off-road with wide, aggressive tread or wheel spacers; if you want zero drama, 265/70R16 or 265/70R17 are the conservative picks. Anything bigger is lift territory. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/3rd-gen/tires/)
- Toyota 4Runner 4th Gen, best years and years to avoid: A 2006–09 V8 is the safest pick. HotCars rates the 2006-on V8 facelift trucks the better buys, Jalopnik says the 2UZ-FE V8 has a reputation for being indestructible (with VVT-i and 270 hp from 2005), and Wikipedia says the V6's revised head gasket arrived late in the 2006 model year. The ones to be careful with are 2003–05 V6s: Autotrader says their head-gasket failures are reported more than average, and Expedition Portal owners put most in 2003–04. Whatever the year, a V8 needs its timing belt at 90,000 miles. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/4th-gen/years/)
- Toyota 4Runner 4th Gen, biggest tire: 265/70R17 (about 31.6 in) is the size the GX 470 community — same chassis and fitment — says fits with no modification, and owners on both platforms report no rubbing on factory wheels. 255/75R17 may need a front fender-liner bolt repositioned. 285/70R17 (about 33 in) needs a body-mount chop and fender-liner work even with a small lift. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/4th-gen/tires/)
- Toyota 4Runner 5th Gen, best years and years to avoid: There's no bad engine year, so buy on condition. Autotrader says the fifth generation has no major issues of concern and recommends a late truck, preferably 2020–2024, which get TSS-P safety tech and CarPlay; it's 'OK' with 2013–2015 and notes owner reports of brake, electrical, rust and paint gripes on 2010–2012. SlashGear singles out 2013–2016 for higher complaint and recall counts. Whatever the year, confirm the Takata airbag (2010–2016) and fuel pump (2014–2015 and 2018–2019) recalls are closed. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/5th-gen/years/)
- Toyota 4Runner 5th Gen, biggest tire: Trail4R's short answer is 32 inches. Stock is 265/70R17 (31.6 in). A 275/70R17 or 255/75R17 (about 32.1 in) shouldn't rub; a 285/70R17 (32.7 in) is 'questionable' and may need a body-mount chop; 255/80R17 (33 in) and anything bigger needs a lift and trimming. Tire brand and wheel offset change the outcome. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/5th-gen/tires/)
- Toyota 4Runner 6th Gen, biggest tire: TRD Off-Road, TRD Pro and Trailhunter trucks already run 33-inch tires (265/70R18) from the factory. SR5 owners on 4Runner6G.com report 285/70R17 (about 33 in) on stock height without rubbing, though they argue about whether the stock 17×7 wheel is too narrow for that tire; one owner saw the tread balloon and moved to 8.5-in-wide wheels. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/6th-gen/tires/)
- Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1st generation), best years and years to avoid: There's no buyer consensus on a best year. In a CK5 thread on which K5 to buy, the owners who pick a first-generation truck do it for the looks and the full-length removable top, and one calls 1971–72 the best looking. The mechanical difference worth knowing is the brakes: 1971 and later trucks have power front discs, while 1969–70 trucks have drums all round unless they've been converted. After that, rust, the top and the quality of past work decide it. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer-1st/years/)
- Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1st generation), biggest tire: On a 67-72 Chevy Trucks thread about a stock 1972 Blazer, several owners run 33x12.50s on 15x8 wheels. Others call 32x11.50 the limit if the springs have sagged. One owner found 33x14.50s rubbed the springs, so width matters as much as height. On CK5, a member calls 33s about 2 inches bigger than stock 31s, fine for a while on the road but likely to hit off-road. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer-1st/tires/)
- Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1973–1991), best years and years to avoid: It depends on what you want. The 1973–75 trucks have the fully open body, which MotorTrend calls the K5's sweet spot for that reason, and 1976–80 trucks are the classic half-cab with the NP205 or NP203 and simpler mechanicals. For a truck to drive, CK5 owners mostly point to the 1987–91 trucks for throttle-body injection, and many name 1989–91 as the best of those for the NP241 transfer case, 30-spline axle shafts and the updated 700R4. Others prefer 1990–91 for the electronic speedometer. Whatever the year, check the frame at the steering box. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer/years/)
- Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1973–1991), biggest tire: About 32 inches. Hogback Fabrication says on CK5 that a stock K5 fits 32s without trimming and 33s with minor trimming. Other owners report 33s rubbing the inner fender at full lock and full bump, but fine on the road. On 16-inch wheels, 285/75R16s are commonly said not to rub. Wheel width and backspacing matter: one member suggests 15x8 wheels at about 3.5 inches of backspacing as the easy fit for 33x12.50s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer/tires/)
- Chevrolet/GMC Suburban (1973–1991 square body), best years and years to avoid: 1987 to 1991. For 1987 all the gasoline engines switched to throttle-body injection, and the 5.7-liter V8 was rated at 210 hp and 300 lb-ft in 10-series trucks. The diesel already had mechanical injection. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/suburban-square/years/)
- Chevrolet/GMC Suburban (1973–1991 square body), biggest tire: On a half-ton, 31x10.50R15s are the safe choice: GMSquarebody owners of a 1987 Suburban 4x4 and a 1987 short-box report no rubbing at all. 33x10.50s on factory rims also work. A moderator ran 33x12.50s on a stock three-quarter-ton Suburban with no rubbing, but says a half-ton will almost certainly need trimming. On CK5, owners of the related half-ton K5 Blazer call 32s safe and say 33s rub at full lock. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/suburban-square/tires/)
- Dodge Ramcharger (first generation), biggest tire: Dodge's largest factory option was a 10-15LT, which the 1978 Macho package used. On Bring a Trailer, listings that mention no lift mostly show 31x10.50R15s. One Top Hand truck ran 32x11.50s, and a 1978 Trail Duster sold on 33x12.50R15s. On a later Ramcharger with the same Dana 44 and leaf-spring layout, an owner found 32x11.50s rubbed when the suspension twisted up. So call 31s safe and 32s the practical limit, and plan on an add-a-leaf or lift before you try 33s off-road. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/ramcharger/ramcharger-1st/tires/)
- Dodge Ramcharger (1981–1993), best years and years to avoid: It depends on what you want. One long-time RamCharger Central member picks 1981–84 for the conventional, non-CAD Dana 44 front axle and 1992–93 for the Magnum engines. Others recommend 1988–93 for fuel injection, which also runs better at steep angles off-road. For the most power and equipment, owners point to a 1993 Canyon Sport with the 5.9 Magnum. Hagerty also rates the late Magnum trucks highest. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/ramcharger/ramcharger-2nd/years/)
- Dodge Ramcharger (1981–1993), biggest tire: About a 32 or a narrow 33. RamCharger Central's Elwenil says 32s fit most Ramchargers with a little rubbing or minor trimming, but the front springs tend to sag, so measure your truck. 33x10.50s on 8-inch-wide wheels are the usual safe choice. Owners disagree about 33x12.50s: one says they rub at full lock, while another ran them on every unlifted Ramcharger he owned. A member survey found 8-inch wheels work and 10-inch wheels rub. 31x10.50s clear with room to flex, and expect 33s to feel slow on stock gears. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/ramcharger/ramcharger-2nd/tires/)
- Ford Bronco (1966–1977), best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus year, and Velocity Restorations says condition matters more than year. It calls 1969–72 'the sweet spot' for the 302 V8 with a vintage feel, and 1973–77 the most refined, with power steering, the automatic and, from 1976, front disc brakes. Autotrader Classics notes the stronger Dana 44 front axle from mid-1971 and that the 1976 steering linkage was poorly received, while CJ Pony Parts calls 1974–75 among the most desirable and most available years. Originality and uncut fenders move the price more than the model year does. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/early-bronco/years/)
- Ford Bronco (1966–1977), biggest tire: On an uncut truck at stock height, Performance Plus Tire calls 30x9.50R15 the safe choice and says 31x10.50R15 may lightly rub at full stuff or full lock. ClassicBroncos owners agree: 235/75R15 bolts on, and a few squeeze 33x9.50s on with fender trimming and some rubbing. For 31–32-inch tires on uncut fenders, plan on a 2–3-inch lift and 3.75–4.25 inches of wheel backspacing; 33x12.50s generally mean cut fenders. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/early-bronco/tires/)
- Ford Full-size Bronco, best years and years to avoid: It depends what you want, because there's no consensus best year: Bronco Zone owners argue engines (the 351 'feels like a truck motor', the 302 is smoother) and OBD-I versus OBD-II rather than model years. The 1978–79 trucks are the only ones with a solid front axle and 400 V8s, and they bring the most money. The 302 got fuel injection in 1985, the 351 and the five-speed manual came in 1988, and four-wheel ABS and a driver's airbag followed in 1993 and 1994. From 1994 the top is effectively fixed, and the 1996 trucks have OBD-II diagnostics. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/full-size/years/)
- Ford Full-size Bronco, biggest tire: A 33-inch tire. On Bronco Zone, one moderator ran 33x12.50R15s on 15x10 wheels on a stock-height 1986 with no rubbing; another owner said 33s fit without a lift but snugly, sometimes needing the bumper ends trimmed or shimmed, with slight radius-arm rub depending on the wheel. For 35s, a 3-inch body lift is the bare minimum, a 4-inch suspension lift is better and 6 inches is ideal. 38s need about 6 inches plus serious fender trimming. Check your axle ratio before going bigger. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/full-size/tires/)
- Ford Bronco II, best years and years to avoid: 1989–1990. The Ranger Station says the 2.9's cylinder heads were redesigned for 1989 (look for '89TM' castings and rectangular rocker pedestals), largely ending the cracking that plagues 1986–88 engines, and that 1989-on A4LD automatics are noticeably better than the 1985–87 units its builder's guide says to stay away from. A late-1990 4x4 may also have the stronger Dana 35 front axle. If you do buy a 1986–88, check the oil for coolant, or for proof the heads have been swapped. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/bronco-ii/years/)
- Ford Bronco II, biggest tire: Stock was 205/75R15, about 27 inches tall. The Ranger Station shows a stock-height Bronco II on 31x10.50R15s with trimmed fenders, and its rule of thumb is that 31s need about 1.5 inches of lift plus fender trimming. 32x11.50R15s have fitted on a 1.5-inch lift with the bottom rear corner of the front fender trimmed. Remember that the Dana 28 front axle is rated for about 31-inch tires. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/bronco-ii/tires/)
- Ford Bronco (sixth generation), best years and years to avoid: Avoid 2021–22 unless the paperwork is perfect: CarGurus says to steer clear of both, and they carry the 2.7 intake-valve recall (24V-635) and the 2026 molded-in-color roof-panel recall. CarGurus calls 2023 the best year, with no investigations and fewer complaints, as long as its recalls are fixed. Later trucks get MIC 2.0 or painted tops, the HOSS 3.0 steering gear on 2024 Badlands and Sasquatch, and a full HOSS 3.0 option for 2025, but 2024–25 trucks have their own front-suspension fastener recalls, so check any year's VIN. Jalopnik, citing Bronco Nation, notes relatively little discussion of failures on the 2.3 four. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/sixth-gen/years/)
- Ford Bronco (sixth generation), biggest tire: On stock wheels and suspension, a 285/75R17 (about 33.8 in) with no rubbing reported. Narrow 35s (35x10.50R17 or 35x11.50R17) fit factory 17s once the front crash bars are removed, usually with a small level of 1.25–1.5 in. Full-width 35x12.50R17s need about +30 mm wheels, high-clearance flares and roughly 1.5–2 in of lift. The factory way to get 35s is the Sasquatch package (315/70R17); the Raptor runs 37s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/sixth-gen/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G-Class W460, biggest tire: About a 32-inch 235/85R16 on the stock steel wheels. An Expedition Portal owner of a short-wheelbase diesel G runs 235/85R16s on standard steel wheels and reports they work well on and off road. The original fitment was a skinny 205 R16, and another owner whose truck came on 215/85R16s is sticking with that size. For 33s and up, plan on lift springs. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w460/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G-Class W461, biggest tire: The G 300 CDI Professional comes on 265/75R16s, about 31.6 inches. On narrow-body Gs, an Expedition Portal owner runs 235/85R16s (about 32 inches) on the standard steel wheels, which is a sensible no-lift ceiling. Beyond that you're into lift springs: GwagenParts' ROGUE spring listing talks about 33- and 35-inch tires, and warns that bigger tires can trigger ABS and ESP warnings. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w461/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G-Class W463, best years and years to avoid: In the US, a 2005–08 G 500. Handsome Motors says the 2002–04 trucks suffer electrical gremlins (seat motors, window regulators, door-lock actuators, transfer-case actuators) that were mostly gone by 2005–06, and Expedition Portal owners tell the same story about 2002–03. CarGurus adds that the very last 1999–2000 Europa G 500s are considered very reliable, and that 2009-on trucks have fewer problems than the early US ones. The 2016–18 twin-turbo trucks are a reliable option, Handsome Motors says, but not the most reliable. In Europe, Autocar's pick is the G 320 CDI. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w463/years/)
- Mercedes-Benz G-Class W463, biggest tire: About 33 inches. Expedition Portal owners report a 275/70R18 on an unlifted G 500 and a 285/65R18 with only a slight rub at full left lock. One owner says he has run 315/75R16s on his G 500 for nearly a decade with no lift and no rubbing, but that's an outlier. Wheel offset matters: one owner's rubbing went away when he swapped ET63 wheels for ET43 G 550 wheels, while another says ET63 wheels tuck the rear tires better on 35s. JWO designed its 4-inch springs specifically to clear tires bigger than 33 inches. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w463/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz 500 GE V8, biggest tire: The factory tire is 265/70R16, about 30.6 inches. On unlifted W463s, Expedition Portal owners run 33-inch tires (275/70R18 and 285/65R18 on 18-inch wheels), with a slight rub at full left lock on the 285s. One owner says up to about 32 inches should clear with no rubbing. On the 500 GE's 16-inch wheels, aim for a similar overall diameter (around 32 inches) and test full lock. Many owners keep these trucks on period-correct 16s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/500ge/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz Europa International Gs, biggest tire: About 33 inches. An Expedition Portal owner runs 275/70R18 on an unlifted 2000 G 500 and only rubbed on aftermarket ET63 wheels. Another runs 285/65R18 with a slight rub at full left lock. Another owner says up to about 32 inches should clear with no rubbing. Have the tire size re-coded with Mercedes diagnostics so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/europa/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 500, best years and years to avoid: 2005–08. The 2002–04 trucks are the ones with the electrical gremlins. Handsome Motors, a G specialist dealer, lists seat motors and controls, window regulators and motors, door-lock actuators and transfer-case actuators, and says the faults got better every year until they were mostly gone by 2005–06. Expedition Portal owners say the same about 2002–03. One owner notes that Mercedes changed some electronics partway through 2003. CarGurus is harsher: it says 2002–05 trucks draw the most complaints, mostly electrical, and that the 2009-on G 550 is better still. Within 2005–08 you're really choosing a gearbox. 2005–06 trucks have the five-speed 722.6 with a dipstick, which one Expedition Portal regular prefers because it's easier to service. 2007–08 trucks have the seven-speed 7G-TRONIC, plus HID lamps and a reversing camera (see the question above for how to tell them apart). Some owners would rather have a pre-2002 Europa G 500 with its manual transfer-case lever and fewer electronics, but parts and paperwork are harder. Whatever the year, test every window, lock and seat before you hand over money. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g500/years/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 500, biggest tire: A 275/70R18 — roughly a 33-inch tire — on the factory 18-inch wheels. Owners on Expedition Portal report it fits an unlifted G 500; one saw rubbing only on aftermarket ET63-offset wheels. A 285/65R18 can rub slightly at full left lock. Re-code the tire size with a Mercedes diagnostic tool so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g500/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 55 AMG, best years and years to avoid: In the US, 2002–2004 G 55s are naturally aspirated (349 hp) and 2005–2011 are Kompressors (469 hp, later 493 and 500 hp). In Europe the supercharger arrived in 2004. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g55-amg/years/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 55 AMG, biggest tire: About 33 inches on 18-inch wheels. Owners of unlifted W463s on Expedition Portal run 275/70R18 with no rubbing on sensible offsets, and 285/65R18 with a slight rub at full left lock. Fitment data lists 285/55R18 for 2004 and 2008 US G 55s, so 18s clear those brakes. One owner warns 18s won't clear G 63 brakes, so test-fit before buying 18s for a 19-inch 2009–2011 truck. Re-code the tire size so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g55-amg/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 550, biggest tire: About 33 inches — a 275/70R18 on 18-inch wheels. A 2014 G 550 owner on Expedition Portal ran BFGoodrich KO2s in that size at stock height with no rubbing at full flex, and a G 500 owner rubbed only on aftermarket ET63-offset wheels (ET43 was fine). A 285/65R18 can rub slightly at full left lock; a 265/65R18 (about 31.6 in) fits with room to spare. Later trucks came on 19s–21s, and owners warn 18s don’t clear every caliper — check before buying wheels, and have the tire size re-coded. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g550/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 63 AMG, best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus best year, so buy on condition. 2016–2018 trucks have 563 hp, new dampers and recalibrated ESP and ABS, and they sell for roughly $15,000 more on Bring a Trailer. 2013–2015 trucks are the bargain. Handsome Motors says the M157 in the G 63 got timing-chain and head-bolt updates, and wants the cooling system and water pump inspected on any of them. Whichever year you buy, make sure the steering-coupling recall (17V250, 2013–2016) is done. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g63-amg/years/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 63 AMG, biggest tire: About 32 inches, on 20-inch wheels. An Expedition Portal owner runs 275/55R20 (about 32 in) on an unlifted G 63, and another 2017 G 63 owner was told by his dealer the size 'will work fine'. Most unlifted W463s fit 33-inch 275/70R18s, but one Expedition Portal member says 18-inch wheels 'will not fit on the G63' over its big front calipers, so try a wheel on the hub before you buy a set. Recode the tyre size so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g63-amg/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 63 AMG 6×6, biggest tire: It comes with 37-inch tyres on 18-inch beadlocks, and Bring a Trailer trucks show 37×12.50R18 tyres. One owner went up to 38×13.50R18 Toyo Open Country M/Ts, along with KW coilovers. There's no known need for anything bigger. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g63-6x6/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G 500 4×4², biggest tire: It doesn't need one — the portal axles are the lift. Stock tires are 325/55R22, about 36 inches tall. When Mercedes showed the truck, it said 37×12.5×18 mud-terrains would be available for production trucks, and its concept photos showed 37-inch mud-terrains on beadlocks. Mercedes-Benz USA says larger off-road tires can be fitted without recalibrating the speedometer, because it reads from the axles. Check caliper clearance before going to 18-inch wheels. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/4x4-squared/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz G-Class (second generation), biggest tire: We couldn’t verify a firm owner consensus for the 2019-on truck. What is documented: factory G 550 sizes are 275/55R19 and 275/50R20 (about 31 in), Mercedes offered 18-inch all-terrain tires as an option, and a 2.5-inch lift kit is rated for up to 33-inch tires. On earlier Gs, about 32 inches is the commonly cited no-rub ceiling — treat it as a starting point and test-fit at full lock. [TO VERIFY FOR 2019+] (https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/second-gen/tires/)
- Ineos Grenadier Station Wagon, best years and years to avoid: There's no bad engine to avoid, since every US truck has the B58. The early US trucks (MY2024) carry all three recalls, so get proof they're closed. MY2026 brings the revised steering, HVAC and driver-assist tweaks plus more than 40 smaller changes. If you plan to drive a lot of highway miles, 2026 is the one to buy. Cars.com calls the 2026 steering 'a tremendous improvement'; Parkers is cooler and calls it 'marginally better on-road'. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/grenadier/station-wagon/years/)
- Ineos Grenadier Station Wagon, biggest tire: From the factory the Grenadier rides on LT265/70R17 or LT255/70R18 (about 32 in.). INEOS Forum owners report 285/70R17 fits with no problem. 285/75R17 (about 34 in.) is the popular sweet spot: owners report no rub on stock suspension, but you'll probably need a couple of washers under the spare carrier to clear the small rear door. DVA Mechanics' fitment guide lists 295/70R17 as 'stock or 40 mm lift' and treats 35-inch tires (315/70R17) as a 2-inch-lift job. A few forum owners report squeezing 35s onto aftermarket wheels without a lift, but treat 285/75R17 as the practical stock limit. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/grenadier/station-wagon/tires/)
- Ineos Grenadier Quartermaster, best years and years to avoid: The engines haven't changed, so the main question is steering. MY2026 trucks have the variable-ratio box, about a 5% tighter turning circle, better HVAC and a quicker way to silence the speed-limit chime. Earlier trucks can be fitted with Owl's steering pump upgrade, which Owl says fits both the Grenadier and Quartermaster. Whichever year you buy, run the VIN for recalls. GearJunkie, which drove both, says the Quartermaster got the same 2026 updates and that with the new steering the long-wheelbase truck drives almost like a normal pickup. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/grenadier/quartermaster/years/)
- Ineos Grenadier Quartermaster, biggest tire: The Quartermaster has the same axles and front suspension as the wagon, and it comes on LT265/70R17 or 255/70R18 (about 32 in.). Wagon owners on the INEOS Forum report 285/70R17 fits without rubbing and 285/75R17 (about 34 in.) fits on stock suspension. DVA Mechanics treats 35s as a 2-inch-lift job. One Quartermaster owner recommends narrow 35s on near-factory offset wheels, such as 255/85R17 or 35×10.5. Because the spare sits in the bed, there's no rear-door clearance problem like on the wagon, but a bigger spare stands taller in the bed. An owner at 7,000 ft stayed at 33s because of power loss on the factory gearing. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/grenadier/quartermaster/tires/)
- AM General Hummer H1, best years and years to avoid: Flash Off-Road says many owners consider the 1998 the quintessential pre-Alpha truck. It has the 1997.5 HVAC, better sound insulation, the 2.56 axles and the last of the Torsen I differentials, before ABS and TorqTrac4 arrived in 1999. Its turbo diesel sits right in the No. 8 crack window, though (see the next question), so test the block or look for a replacement engine. Flash Off-Road calls the 2004, with its new interior, Optimizer engine and optional Eaton lockers, the best stock truck yet, and says 2004 is a big step up from 2001 for noise and comfort. The 2006 Alpha is 'an order of magnitude better' on and off road. Autotrader calls it the ultimate H1, and Hagerty found Alphas worth over 40% more than a comparable 2004. The 1992–93 6.2 trucks are simple and a favorite of hard-core off-roaders, but slow. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/h1/years/)
- AM General Hummer H1, biggest tire: The factory tire was a 37x12.50R16.5, and later trucks used 37-inch tires on 17-inch wheels. Flash Off-Road says a 38x15.5 is the largest you can run on stock wheels without lifting the truck, though you need to watch for rubbing on the suspension at full lock. Taller tires need a body lift: Flash Off-Road reports owners running 39.5s with a 2-inch body lift and no rubbing. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/h1/tires/)
- AM General Hummer H2, best years and years to avoid: If budget allows, 2008–09 for the 6.2, the six-speed and the much better interior; owners say they're better in every way. They're also the rarest and most expensive, and some of their parts are specific to those years. Among 2003–07 trucks, one owner would pick a mid-2005 to 2007 truck over a 2003 for the stronger front diff and better build. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/h2/years/)
- AM General Hummer H2, biggest tire: Owners agree on 37x12.50R17 on stock wheels, or wheels with the same offset. One owner runs Cooper STTs at stock height with a slight torsion-bar crank and doesn't rub at full stuff, apart from a light scrub on the sway bar at full lock, which the stock 35s do too. 37x14.50s didn't fit. Wider tires or different offsets need a lift, spacers or both. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/h2/tires/)
- International Scout 80 / 800, best years and years to avoid: There's no agreed best year: rust decides, and an early Scout with a rotten frame is the expensive mistake. If you're choosing, the 800A (from late 1968) brought the Dana 20 transfer case and a Dana 44 rear axle, and the V8s are the ones for highway speed. Cars Counsel rates every 80 and 800 'good with inspection' because of parts scarcity and age. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-80-800/years/)
- International Scout 80 / 800, biggest tire: We couldn't find a forum consensus for a bone-stock 80 or 800. The best data point comes from IH Parts America, which says "a 31" tire should fit fine" with its CPT spring system. That system adds 1 to 3 inches, about 2 on most trucks, and IHPA's own 800B runs 31x10.50 Duratracs on Scout II rally wheels. IHPA also notes that the front tires can hit the rear of the front wheel well, which its reverse-shackle kit addresses by moving the axle forward. So on stock springs, stay close to stock size. With fresh lift springs, 31s are the realistic ceiling. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-80-800/tires/)
- International Scout II, best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus year, and rust matters more than any of them. After 1974 every Scout II has Dana 44s at both ends and power front discs. Moses Ludel of 4WD Mechanix calls 1979 'a good model year' and says the only advantage of a 1980 is the one-year Dana 300 transfer case with its lower low range. Hagerty says the 1977–79 Super Scout II is the most valuable. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-ii/years/)
- International Scout II, biggest tire: There's no clean stock answer, because 31s are already marginal. One owner of a 1977 Scout II said his 31s rubbed. IH Parts America's owner recommends a reverse-shackle kit and a 2.5-inch spring lift to run 31s without rubbing, and at least a 1-inch body lift plus a steering upgrade for 33s. Anything Scout rates the Rough Country 2.5-inch kit for up to a 32-inch tire. Plan on stock-sized tires (around 30 inches) if you won't lift it. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-ii/tires/)
- International Scout Motors Traveler & Terra, biggest tire: Unknown, because production specifications haven't been published. The concepts were shown on 35-inch tires (Traveler) and 37-inch tires on 18-inch wheels (Terra, November 2025 LA Auto Show). (https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-motors/tires/)
- Isuzu Trooper (first generation), biggest tire: The factory size from 1987 was P235/75R15, about 29 inches, on 6.0- or 6.5-inch-wide 15-inch wheels. We couldn't verify a first-generation forum consensus for the largest no-lift size, so check the tire-fitment chart and build threads on Planet Isuzoo before you buy, and check the rear-door-mounted spare carrier too. Wheels are 6 x 139.7 mm with a 100 mm center bore and M12 x 1.5 studs. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/trooper-1/tires/)
- Isuzu Trooper (second generation), best years and years to avoid: There's no clear sweet spot. The 1992–97 3.2 avoids the 3.5's oil appetite: one Overland Bound owner says the 3.2 'never had an oil consumption issue' and the 1998–2002 3.5s 'did have a bit'. NHTSA's complaint files peak with the 1999 model, and CarComplaints rates 2000 as the worst year, mainly for transmission failures. The 3.5 is the stronger engine, so if you want one, buy on oil-use history and receipts rather than the year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/trooper-2/years/)
- Isuzu Trooper (second generation), biggest tire: Owners put it at about 33 inches. An Overland Bound owner says you can fit 33s before you need a lift, citing a chart on Planet Isuzoo, and an Expedition Portal member says 285/75R16 fits with no lift. Stock was P245/70R16 on 16 x 7 wheels (Acura SLX spec). The bolt pattern is 6 x 139.7 mm with a 100 mm center bore; one owner runs wheels from a 2014 Toyota 4Runner. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/trooper-2/tires/)
- Jeep CJ-5, best years and years to avoid: Condition beats year on a truck this old, but there are two sensible targets. Hagerty would aim for an AMC-era 232 or 258 six from 1972 on, for smooth power and cheaper running than the V8. Jeep-CJ.com and The Drive both rate the Buick Dauntless V6 (optional 1965–71) as strong. The one to skip is a 1980–83 truck with the GM Iron Duke four, which Jeep-CJ.com calls particularly weak; the optional 258 those years is fine. The Drive adds that pre-1976 open frames tend to crack and later boxed frames tend to rust, so check either kind. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-5/years/)
- Jeep CJ-5, biggest tire: In a Jeep-CJ.com thread on stock CJs, members (one running a '79 CJ-5) put 31-inch tires as the safe maximum: one says '31's without rubbing,' and another says 32s rub the rear wheel wells. A little trimming can make 32s fit, but there isn't much to trim ahead of the rear wheels, and most doubt 33s will fit. Old springs sag, so 31s may be the practical limit. Wide tires may need wheels with less backspacing to clear the springs and fenders at full lock. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-5/tires/)
- Jeep CJ-7, best years and years to avoid: There's no single answer, so we don't flag one. Owners on Off-Road.com split between 1976–79 trucks, for the T-18 four-speed and the 304 V8 option, and 1982-on trucks with the wider-track axles; a 1986 with the factory Dana 44 rear is a good find. Jeep-CJ.com calls the T-18 the best CJ manual and says to avoid the GM Iron Duke four used from 1980 to 1983. The Drive says to watch out for Quadra-Trac. Buy the best frame you can find, then pick the drivetrain. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-7/years/)
- Jeep CJ-7, biggest tire: A 31x10.50R15 on the right wheel, on a healthy stock CJ-7. Performance Plus Tire's guide says it needs healthy springs and shallow backspacing (about 3.5 in on a 15x8 for narrow-track trucks), and JeepCJ.com owners agree 31s are the practical limit. One member reported 32x11.50s on a stock CJ with very little rubbing. 33x12.50R15s need a lift; most CJs running 33s have about 4 inches of spring lift, though 2.5 inches can work with the right backspacing and some fender trimming. Every CJ-7 used 15-inch wheels on a 5 x 5.5 in bolt pattern, with factory sizes from H78-15 bias-plies to metric radials up to 235/75R15 (Performance Plus). (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-7/tires/)
- Jeep CJ-8 Scrambler, biggest tire: Jeep-CJ.com members put 31-inch tires as the safe maximum on a stock CJ. They say 32s rub the rear wheel wells without trimming, and doubt 33s will fit. The thread covers CJs generally rather than the Scrambler specifically, but the CJ-8 shares the CJ-7's front end and springs. Saggy old springs and wheel backspacing can make even 31s tight. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-8/tires/)
- Jeep Wagoneer & Cherokee (SJ), biggest tire: We couldn't find a forum consensus we trust for unlifted SJs, so we won't guess. Tire databases list 225/75R15 for 1976–83 Wagoneers (235/70R15 is also listed for 1976). The Cherokee Chief's wider axles and bigger fender flares were added so it could run larger tires. For anything bigger, test-fit at full lock and with the suspension compressed, or add a modest leaf-spring lift. Running bigger tires on yours? Tell us through Show Us Your Rig. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/sj-wagoneer/tires/)
- Jeep Grand Wagoneer (SJ), best years and years to avoid: 1989–91, if you can. Those years got better rust-proofing (electrocoat primer), base-clear paint, an improved A/C compressor, an overhead console, keyless entry and a rear wiper. The 1991 Final Edition carries a premium. Hagerty's specialist adds that low mileage, under about 100,000, is the safest buy. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-wagoneer/years/)
- Jeep Grand Wagoneer (SJ), biggest tire: We couldn't find a forum consensus we trust for the SJ, so we won't guess. The factory size is P235/75R15 on 15x7 six-lug alloys (1989 spec). Anything larger should be test-fitted at full lock and with the suspension compressed. Team Grand Wagoneer sells a 3-inch lift kit with springs and shocks for owners who want more. Running bigger tires on yours? Tell us through Show Us Your Rig. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-wagoneer/tires/)
- Jeep Cherokee XJ, best years and years to avoid: Buy a 4.0. OffroadXtreme recommends the 1991-and-later HO, says 1987–90 Renix trucks suit owners who like diagnosing sensors, and says to avoid 1984–86 (no 4.0). NAXJA members single out non-ABS 1998–99 trucks with the 4.0, AW4, NP231 and 29-spline 8.25 as about the most solid combination. The 2000–01 trucks are good if the head has been checked or replaced. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cherokee-xj/years/)
- Jeep Cherokee XJ, biggest tire: In a NAXJA thread, members agree a 235/75R15 (about 29 in) on the stock 15x7 wheels with 5.25 in backspacing fits fine, and treat a 30x9.50R15 as the practical limit. One owner's '88 on 30x9.50s rubbed only the front control arms at full lock, which a steering-stop adjustment fixes at the cost of turning circle. A 255/70R16 (about 30 in) rubbed the rear fenders on a loaded 2000. Less backspacing pushes the tire out toward the flares. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cherokee-xj/tires/)
- Jeep Comanche MJ, best years and years to avoid: Buy a 4.0, ideally a 1991–92 HO: 190 hp and Chrysler's easier-to-diagnose engine management, the same reason Off Road Xtreme recommends the HO in the XJ. 1987–90 Renix trucks are good too, but they're diagnosed with a multimeter. 1986 trucks have no 4.0. If you do buy a 2.5, Comanche Club members say look for 4.10 or 4.56 gears. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/comanche-mj/years/)
- Jeep Comanche MJ, biggest tire: The MJ's front end and fenders are the XJ's, so XJ consensus is a fair guide: a 235/75R15 (about 29 in) on the stock 15 in wheels fits, and a 30x9.50R15 is the practical limit, possibly rubbing the front lower control arms at full lock. NAXJA posters say a 31x10.50 needs bump stops or trimming. We found no separate MJ-only consensus. Load the bed before judging rear clearance. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/comanche-mj/tires/)
- Jeep Wrangler YJ, best years and years to avoid: Sources disagree. 4WD Mechanix says 1987–92 YJs used a slave cylinder built into the release bearing and that 1993 brought the external slave and pivot arm used in the TJ. Wikipedia dates the move outside the bellhousing to 1994, and Advance Adapters lists its internal-bearing hose kit for 1987–93. Treat 1993 as either, and look for an external slave on the bellhousing. The internal type means pulling the transmission to replace it. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/yj/years/)
- Jeep Wrangler YJ, biggest tire: A stock YJ usually takes 30-inch tires on stock rims without trouble. Four Wheel Trends says 31x10.50s can be squeezed on, but they may need wheels with different backspacing and can still rub, so don't wheel that setup hard without a lift. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/yj/tires/)
- Jeep Grand Cherokee ZJ, best years and years to avoid: There's no real consensus, so we don't flag one. SlashGear picks 1993, 1994 and 1998 and says to avoid 1995–96 for transmission complaints, but NHTSA's complaint database holds a similar 1,200 to 1,560 complaints for every ZJ model year, with 1998 logging the most powertrain reports, and CarComplaints.com shows no ZJ year standing out. Buy on condition instead: frame rust, leaks, a transfer case that works in every mode and the 13V-252 hitch recall done. If you want the collectible, it's the 1998 5.9 Limited. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-cherokee-zj/years/)
- Jeep Grand Cherokee ZJ, biggest tire: About 30 in. Factory sizes ran from 215/75R15 to 245/70R15 and 225/70R16, all roughly 28 in tall. A 30x9.50R15 is the practical limit on stock springs: one owner ran 30x9.50 BFGoodrich all-terrains on a stock '93 and said they came close to rubbing but didn't. Rough Country and Zone rate their 1.5–2 in spacer lifts for 30x9.50s, and Rough Country's 3.5 in kit for 31x10.50s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-cherokee-zj/tires/)
- Jeep Wrangler TJ, best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus year, which is why we only flag the early trucks. SlashGear rates mid-to-late TJs among the most desirable Wranglers and points manual buyers to 2005–06 for the NSG370 six-speed. RealTruck, on the other hand, lists 2005 and 2006 among its worst Wrangler years, and Quadratec says 2005–06 4.0s need the oil pump drive assembly checked or replaced. Driving Line doesn't pick a year at all: it says get the six-cylinder. Every TJ frame can rust, so the frame matters more than the model year. Check the rear lower control-arm mounts first. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj/years/)
- Jeep Wrangler TJ, biggest tire: Four Wheel Trends says the biggest tire you can generally run on a stock TJ and keep full function is a 31x10.50-15, and that even that size may rub at full flex, which a washer or two on the steering stops usually cures. The Rubicon came from the factory on 31-inch LT245/75R16 Goodyear MT/Rs. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj/tires/)
- Jeep Wrangler Unlimited (LJ), best years and years to avoid: 2005–06 brought the NSG370 six-speed manual. Those years also need the OPDA checked. The 2005–06 Rubicon Unlimited is the one with front and rear Dana 44s, air lockers and the 4:1 Rock-Trac. A 2004 or non-Rubicon LJ still has the Dana 44 rear and is a better starting point for a build than a Dana 35 TJ. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj-unlimited/years/)
- Jeep Wrangler Unlimited (LJ), biggest tire: The LJ uses the TJ's axles, flares and suspension, so the TJ answer applies: Four Wheel Trends puts the stock-suspension limit at about a 31x10.50, which may still rub at full flex until you add a washer or two to the steering stops. Jeep itself sent the Rubicon Unlimited out on LT245/75R16 (about 31-inch) tires at stock height. For 33s, plan on a lift; Quadratec's buyer's guide pairs 33s with a 3-inch-class suspension lift. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj-unlimited/tires/)
- Jeep Wrangler JK (2-door), best years and years to avoid: A 2012-on Pentastar. Quadratec calls it a generally strong engine, while Driving Line says the 2007–11 3.8 burns oil, leaks intake gaskets and cracks exhaust manifolds, and has seen some spin bearings by 100,000 miles. Driving Line's daily-driver pick is 2013 or newer; SlashGear rates 2012–13 as the standout years. The year to be wary of is 2007: several first-year recalls, and CarComplaints.com logs more complaints for 2007 and 2008 than for any other Wrangler year. Not everyone agrees on the Pentastar's first years, either: RealTruck lists 2012–14 among its worst, citing engine complaints. So on a 2012–13 ask about the left cylinder head, and on any Pentastar check the oil filter housing. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk/years/)
- Jeep Wrangler JK (2-door), biggest tire: 33 inches is the usual answer, with caveats. ExtremeTerrain says many JK owners fit 33s on a stock suspension, but fender rubbing will probably show up off-road at full flex, and width matters as much as height. On JK-Forum, owners of stock two-door Rubicons report 285/75R17s clearing on pavement, with rubbing on the control arms at full lock that adjusting the steering stops can cure. Not every wheel works: one owner couldn't fit 285/75R17s on AEV Pintlers without a lift. 255-width 33s are the safe bet; 35s need a lift. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk/tires/)
- Jeep Wrangler JK Unlimited, best years and years to avoid: A 2012-on Pentastar. Quadratec calls it a generally strong engine, while Driving Line says the 2007–11 3.8 burns oil, leaks intake gaskets and cracks exhaust manifolds, and has seen some spin bearings by 100,000 miles. Driving Line's daily-driver pick is 2013 or newer; SlashGear rates 2012–13 as the standout years. The year to be wary of is 2007: several first-year recalls, and CarComplaints.com logs more complaints for 2007 and 2008 than for any other Wrangler year. Not everyone agrees on the Pentastar's first years, either: RealTruck lists 2012–14 among its worst, citing engine complaints. So on a 2012–13 ask about the left cylinder head, and on any Pentastar check the oil filter housing. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk-unlimited/years/)
- Jeep Wrangler JK Unlimited, biggest tire: 33s. JK-Forum owners agree that most 285/70R17s (about 33 inches) fit on stock wheels, at stock height, with the stock bump stops. Expect light rubbing at full lock and at full flex, where they touch the flares, liners and sometimes the front sway bar. A steering-stop washer and the right backspacing help. ExtremeTerrain says 35s need at least a 2–3-inch lift, the right wheel offset and possibly new gears. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk-unlimited/tires/)
- Jeep Wrangler JL, best years and years to avoid: 2018, mainly. SlashGear counted 11 recalls and more than 1,000 owner complaints for the 2018 Wrangler, most about wandering at highway speed, and says steering complaints carried on, less often, for two more years. NHTSA's 2018 list includes track-bar bracket welds (18V-675, also 2019), the intermediate steering shaft (18V-343) and rear frame-rail corrosion (18V-231), and manual trucks from 2018 on are covered by the clutch recalls (20V-124, 21V-028, 23V-116). Quadratec says Jeep later moved from aluminum to cast-iron steering boxes. No later year is a write-off: buy any JL with its recalls and steering fixes documented. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jl/years/)
- Jeep Wrangler JL, biggest tire: On a Rubicon, 35s. Driving Line ran 35x12.50R17s on a stock-height JL Rubicon with JKS bump-stop spacers and the stock flares. They cleared on level ground but hit the inner fenders when flexed, and the spacers cost about 2 inches of up-travel. On a Sport or Sahara, the realistic answer is a 33 with a wheel change; 35s on those trims usually need bump stops, less backspacing and often a 2–2.5-inch lift. Driving Line's test truck was a four-door, but the two-door uses the same axles and flares. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jl/tires/)
- Jeep Wrangler JL Unlimited, best years and years to avoid: No year is the consensus pick, so we don't flag one. The one to be wary of is 2018: SlashGear counted 11 recalls and more than 1,000 complaints, mostly about highway wander, and NHTSA's list includes track-bar bracket welds (18V-675, 2018–19), the steering shaft (18V-343) and rear frame-rail corrosion (18V-231). SlashGear calls 2020-on trucks the more enticing buy for their engine choices, but each brings its own recalls: EcoDiesel fuel pumps (22V-767, 23V-263), 4xe high-voltage batteries (23V-787, 25V-741) and, on 2021–25 trucks, the power-steering pump wiring (26V-363). Buy the truck whose recall list you can see closed. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jl-unlimited/years/)
- Jeep Wrangler JL Unlimited, biggest tire: On a Rubicon, 35s. Driving Line ran 35x12.50R17s on a stock-height JL Unlimited Rubicon with bump-stop spacers and the factory flares. They cleared on level ground but hit the inner fenders when flexed. Performance Plus Tire says Jeep ships the Rubicon 392 on LT315/70R17s, which are nearly 35s (check early 392s: the 35s were also part of the optional Xtreme Recon package). Performance Plus Tire says a Rubicon 4xe has about 2.1 inches less clearance than the gas Rubicon, so it needs bump-stop extensions for 35s. On a Sport or Sahara, stay with 33s and a wheel change, or lift 2–2.5 inches for 35s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jl-unlimited/tires/)
- Jeep Gladiator JT, best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus year yet, so we don't flag one. The recall history is the better guide. Early 2020 trucks had the rear driveshaft recall (19V-636). Manual trucks from 2020 to 2023 are covered by the clutch pressure-plate recalls (20V-124, 21V-028, 23V-116), and some 2021s needed a second fix (24V-572). Diesels have fuel-pump recalls 22V-767 (2021–22) and 23V-263 (2021–23), and 2021–25 trucks are in the power-steering pump wiring recall (26V-363). The 2024 refresh added curtain airbags and the big screen, if those matter to you. Buy whichever year you can prove every recall on. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/gladiator-jt/years/)
- Jeep Gladiator JT, biggest tire: On a Rubicon or Mojave, a 35x11.50R17 on the stock 17x7.5 wheel, per Drivingline's Rubicon fitment guide, which also says 37s need at least a 1-inch front spacer and bump stops and still rub off-road.
