On Sport and Sport S trucks, JeepGladiatorForum owners run 33s (285/70R17) without rubbing. Some say 35s work on stock suspension with little rubbing; others say they hit the flares at full flex. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/gladiator-jt/tires/)
- Jeep Wagoneer & Grand Wagoneer (WS), biggest tire: We couldn't find an owner consensus we trust yet, so we won't guess. Factory sizes are 275/65R18 all-terrains with the Advanced All-Terrain Group, 275/55R20 and 285/45R22, on a 6x139.7 bolt pattern. Limitless Tire's fitment guide lists 275–305 mm widths on 18- to 26-inch wheels. Test-fit anything taller at full lock in Off-Road 2 and at Park height, because the air suspension drops the body 1.6 inches. Running bigger tires on yours? Tell us. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/wagoneer-ws/tires/)
- Lada Niva (VAZ-2121 / 4x4 Legend), best years and years to avoid: In the US, only trucks over 25 years old can be imported, so the choice is a 1.6 VAZ-2121 (four-speed, through 1993) or an early 1.7 21213 or 21214 (five-speed, from 1993–94). The 1.7s are torquier and have the low-lip tailgate, while the pre-1985 trucks with chrome trim are the collector pieces. Wikipedia mentions a 1980 truck that sold in Russia for 3.2 million roubles in 2016. Elsewhere, the 2009–2011 21214M updates, ABS from late 2011 and the maintenance-free hubs from October 2016 make later trucks easier to live with. Whatever the year, the best Niva is the least rusty one. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/niva/niva/years/)
- Lada Niva (VAZ-2121 / 4x4 Legend), biggest tire: About 27–27.5 inches. Stock is 185/75R16 (175/80R16 on early trucks), roughly 26.9–27.0 in tall. NIVA-FAQ owners report that on 15-inch wheels a 205/70R15 clears on the right offset, but a 205/75R15 rubs the front of the arch at full lock and the rear arch at full droop. Size for size, a 205/70R16 (27.3 in) is about the limit. The factory Bronto runs 235/75R16s, but only with 35 mm more ground clearance. BaT's 1993 Niva on oversized 15s 'rubs on the wheel wells'. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/niva/niva/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser J20 / J25 (FJ25), biggest tire: There's no forum consensus for the FJ25, and the bigger problem is wheels. Restored trucks on Bring a Trailer have worn 6.00-16 military-style tires, and one 1959 ran 265/75R16 all-terrains on its 16-inch steel wheels. IH8MUD members warn that 15-inch disc-brake wheels hit the FJ25's tie-rod ends and 15-inch drum wheels won't clear the drum rivets. Stay with 16-inch wheels and a period-sized tire unless you want to start modifying the truck. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj25/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser FJ40, best years and years to avoid: Most buyers prefer 1976-and-later trucks for front disc brakes and the 4.2 L 2F. 1979 added optional power steering and A/C and taller 3.70 gears in the US. IH8MUD veterans like the '78 and would consider 1979–83 at the right price, but note that 1980-and-later bodies seem to rust more readily. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj40/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser FJ40, biggest tire: The 'old tried and true' answer on IH8MUD is 31x10.50R15 on stock wheels and suspension. 33x9.50R15 is a popular size on stock 15-inch rims too, but owners report rubbing at the rear over bumps or at full flex. One fixed it with 1-inch spacers under the bump stops, and another had to adjust the front steering stops. One member said 33x10.50s looked 'pretty stuffed.' (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj40/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser FJ45 / FJ55, best years and years to avoid: There's no settled answer. Later trucks have the 4.2 L 2F, a four-speed and front disc brakes (the domed hood is the easy tell), and factory power steering came at the very end. Even IH8MUD members disagree on exactly when those arrived, with some 1974–75 trucks carrying odd mixes of parts. Earlier trucks use the 3.9 L F and a three-speed whose first gear has no synchro, which some collectors prefer for originality. Owners agree on one thing: rust is your biggest enemy, so buy the straightest body you can find. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj45-fj55/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser FJ45 / FJ55, biggest tire: We couldn't find a solid FJ55- or FJ45-specific consensus. They use 40 Series axles, and for the stock FJ40, IH8MUD's 'tried and true' size is 31x10.50R15, with 33x9.50R15 fitting but rubbing at full flex. Try any size on your own truck before committing. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj45-fj55/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser FJ60, biggest tire: 33x9.50 fits on stock suspension; one IH8MUD member runs them on a stock FJ62 with 240,000 miles. 33x10.50 might fit, but 33x12.50s won't without a lift: one '87 FJ60 on a 2.5-inch BDS lift still rubbed its inner wheel wells at full stuff. Corsetti runs 31x10.50R15s on stock springs and says not to go wider than 10.5 in or taller than 33 in on a factory rim; Cruiser Corps also advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on the 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj60/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser FJ62, biggest tire: On a stock FJ62, one IH8MUD member runs 33x9.50s with no problems. 33x10.50 might fit, but 33x12.50s won't without a lift. Many owners choose 31x10.50R15, which looks right at stock height or on an OME lift. Corsetti says not to go wider than 10.5 in or taller than 33 in on a factory rim, and Cruiser Corps advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on the 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj62/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 70 Series, best years and years to avoid: Unsealed 4X4 says many enthusiasts prefer the 2007–2016 V8s, which don't have a DPF, but that service history matters more than the year. For US imports, the age rule means older trucks, typically with the 1HZ, 2H, 3B or 13B-T diesels or the 3F and 1FZ petrol sixes. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/70-series/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 70 Series, biggest tire: The IH8MUD consensus for a stock-height long-wheelbase 70 is 235/85R16, about 31.7 inches. 285/75R16 (33 inches) will go on, but on factory steel wheels owners report it rubs on the inside at full lock unless you change wheel offset. Short-wheelbase owners in the same thread treat 255/85R16 (about 33 inches) as the sensible upper limit, and the one running them has a lift. Sagging old springs make everything rub sooner. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/70-series/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 80 Series, best years and years to avoid: For most people, a 1993–97 FZJ80. On IH8MUD the advice is consistent: the 4.5 L 1FZ-FE makes 212 hp against the 3F-E's 155 (one member calls the 3F-E 'a relic'), it could be ordered with front and rear lockers, and ABS trucks got a full-float rear with disc brakes. Owners there say the 1995–97 changes (airbags, new dash, OBD-II, the A343F) are small next to the 1993 engine switch, so condition and lockers matter more than which FZJ80 year it is. The trade-off is the 1FZ-FE's head gasket, which owners treat as part of owning one. The 1991–92 FJ80 is simpler and cheaper but slower, with a semi-float rear and drum brakes. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/80-series/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 80 Series, biggest tire: The safe answer from IH8MUD is 285/75R16, about 33 inches, which fits a stock 80 without drama. Owners also report 305/70R16 and 295/75R16 fitting, though wheel width and offset matter as much as the tire size. 35s 'fit, but rub like mad' on a stock truck. Christo Slee's advice is that 35s work with a 2-inch Old Man Emu lift, but you'll probably rub at full flex unless you lower the bump stops. Stock size is 275/70R16. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/80-series/tires/)
- Toyota Mega Cruiser, biggest tire: It already wears 37s. Japanese sources give the factory tire as 37x12.50R17.5 LT, and BaT trucks run 37x12.50 tires on 17-inch steel or aftermarket wheels. We found no owner reports of going bigger. With hub reduction and 420 mm of clearance, it doesn't need more. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/mega-cruiser/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 90, biggest tire: 265/75R16 (about 31.6 in). An IH8MUD member who has owned both a 90 and a 95 says it won't rub on stock suspension unless the springs have sagged, and ExplorOz members add that it needs the 7-inch rims of a GXL-type truck, because it's too wide for the 6-inch rims on base models. 285/75R16 rubs with or without a lift, on the upper control arm and a rear pinch weld. For 33s, the same IH8MUD member suggests a lift and 255/85R16s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-90/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 100 Series, best years and years to avoid: If you want the best road truck, 2003–07. IH8MUD's new-owner thread lists the five-speed A750F as the reason, and several owners there reckon the gearbox is a bigger step than the 2006–07 VVT-i engine's extra power, which costs a lot more. On Expedition Portal, one owner calls 2003–05 'THE years' and warns that the VVT-i trucks' air-injection system is expensive to fix. 1998–99 trucks are the only ones with the optional rear locker, but they also have the two-pinion front diff and, Slee notes, throttle-sensor faults. Condition and the timing-belt history matter more than any year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/100-series/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 100 Series, biggest tire: The 100-series FAQ answer on IH8MUD is 285/75R16 on 16-inch wheels or 285/65R18 on 18s, both about 33 inches. 295/75R16s do fit, with half an inch to an inch of clearance at full turn, but owners call it tight. Even 285/75s can be snug at the rear: one owner measured 3/4 inch to the plastic wheel-well liner. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/100-series/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 120, best years and years to avoid: For a V6, anything from late 2005: 4X4 Australia says to skip the earlier four-speed autos and buy a five-speed. For the 1KD-FTV diesel, AustralianCar.Reviews says aluminium injector seats replaced the failure-prone copper ones from August 2007, so a later truck, or an earlier one with receipts for new seats, is the safer buy. 4X4 Australia calls the 2006–08 trucks the high point of the model's reputation. Either way, service records beat the build date. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-120/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 120, biggest tire: The stock size is 265/65R17 on a 7.5Jx17 +30 wheel. ExplorOz owners run 265/70R17 'with no rubbing issues', which matches the GX 470 consensus on the same chassis. 285/70R17 (about 33 in) needs at least a 50 mm (2 in) lift and +50 offset wheels, or some trimming of the body mount behind the mud flap. On 16-inch wheels, a 265/70R16 is a common upsize, but one owner says 16s may need caliper grinding on a 120. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-120/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 200 Series, best years and years to avoid: Unsealed 4X4 says many buyers see 2012–15 as the sweet spot: updated over the early trucks, but before the DPF that arrived on diesels in late 2015. On IH8MUD, owners point US shoppers to 2013–15 trucks, which have taken most of the depreciation, while 2016–21 add the eight-speed and more safety kit (one owner adds that the eight-speed didn't improve fuel economy much). Unsealed's last word applies everywhere: service history matters more than the model year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/200-series/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 200 Series, biggest tire: On IH8MUD, one owner says 285/65R18 'will fit fine with zero rubbing' on a stock truck and 285/70R18 'will rub a bit but should be manageable'; others in the same thread report the 285/70 needs heat-gunning and trimming of the plastic, so treat 285/65R18 as the no-work size. One owner running 285/70R17s on aftermarket wheels reported light rubbing on the plastic liner, fixed with a heat gun. The tire-database thread calls 275/70s 'tried and true'. For anything bigger, check the forum's 200 Series Tire and Wheel Size Database. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/200-series/tires/)
- Toyota FJ Cruiser, best years and years to avoid: 2010–14 if you can. Those trucks have the dual VVT-i engine on regular fuel, and CarGurus says the inner-fender bulge mostly shows up on 2007–09 trucks, while 2007 draws far more owner complaints than any other year. IH8MUD owners add that some pre-February 2007 builds had a brittle rear ring and pinion, so check the door-jamb build date. They also point out that an early truck you plan to re-gear anyway isn't much of a loss. Rust history and how the truck was used matter more than the year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj-cruiser/years/)
- Toyota FJ Cruiser, biggest tire: About a 285/70R17 (roughly 33 x 11 inches). One owner on stock suspension found his only rubbed the driver's-side mud flap under compression and fixed it by heating and flattening the flap. A long-time IH8MUD member's stricter view is that only a 31–32 inch tire clears in every situation; above that you need a body mount chop. Width and wheel backspacing matter as much as diameter, because the inside of the tire hits the front body mount at full lock. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj-cruiser/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 150, best years and years to avoid: Unsealed 4X4's summary: 2009–2012 are cheaper but have the early issues, 2013–2015 are a sweet spot for many buyers, 2015–2019 get the 2.8 but in the early DPF era, and 2020-on are the most desirable, with 150 kW and CarPlay. It also flags 2009 and 2017 for electrical gremlins. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-150/years/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 150, biggest tire: Owner consensus on the Lexus GX 460, the US twin with the same body and suspension, is about 32 inches. 255/70R18 fits with no rubbing, 265/70R18 touches the plastics at full lock, and on 17s a 275/65R17 shows only a slight liner rub at full turn. Prado bumpers and grades differ, so test-fit before you buy. 33s need a lift, and 35s need a 2–2.5 in lift plus upper control arms, a body-mount chop and trimming. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-150/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 250 Series, biggest tire: Factory tires are about 31.5 inches on the 1958 and 32.6 inches on the other grades. Threepiece's fitment guide shows 275/70R18s (about 33 inches) on stock wheels and suspension with plenty of clearance and no trimming. Owners go a bit bigger: 285/70R18s (about 33.7 inches) on stock suspension, including one reported on 18x9 +40 wheels with no rubbing on gentle trails. An LT275/70R18 KO3 (33.2 inches) just fits in the spare well. 35s are possible on stock suspension, but only after removing the mud flaps, crush brackets and canards, heat-forming the fender liners and choosing the right wheel offset. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/250-series/tires/)
- Toyota Land Cruiser 300 Series, biggest tire: IH8MUD owners report 275/70R18 (about 33.3 inches) and 285/70R18 KO3s (about 33.7 inches) with no rubbing on stock suspension. One LX owner with 275/70R18s had no rub at any AHC height, at full lock, in drive or reverse. 295/70R18s on stock wheels have been reported on an LX 700h Overtrail, and Dissent Off-Road told a member that 35s on a +40 mm offset wheel fit with minimal to zero trimming. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/300-series/tires/)
- Land Rover Series I–III, best years and years to avoid: Depends what you want. Series Is are the collectors' trucks. Classic Car Hub calls an 88- or 109-inch Series IIA the sweet spot, with good parts supply and a well-documented spec. Octane says the Series III is by far the easiest to live with and recommends a short-wheelbase 2.25 petrol for most buyers, or a Stage 1 V8 if you want something special; Series123 notes the III's gearbox isn't as strong as the II's. Heritage Parts Centre also rates the 2.25 petrol the preferable engine. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/series/years/)
- Land Rover Series I–III, biggest tire: 235/85R16 is the size most owners recommend: a Rovers North forum member calls it close to, but a little wider than, the factory-optional 7.50x16, and it should fit a stock 88 or 109 once the steering stops are adjusted so the tyre clears the frame at full lock (expect a slightly bigger turning circle). 215/85R16 is also close to 7.50x16. 265/75R16 on stock 5.5-inch rims rubbed the frame by about half to three-quarters of an inch for one owner, and another found 265s too wide on a 109. Original rims are tube-type, so check the wheels before fitting tubeless radials. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/series/tires/)
- Land Rover 90 / 110 / Defender, best years and years to avoid: For a 25-year-legal import, the Tdi years. ECD rates the 300Tdi (1994–98) the top choice for longevity and the 200Tdi (1990–94) a close second, and Classic Car Hub says if you remember one engine number, make it 300Tdi. Early '10P' Td5s have known head and oil-pump-drive problems, so look for a 15P engine or proof of repair. Among the Puma trucks, PistonHeads points to a 2011. Whatever the engine, the chassis, bulkhead and rear crossmember decide what it's worth. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/defender-90-110/years/)
- Land Rover 90 / 110 / Defender, biggest tire: 235/85R16 is the classic factory size on 110s and the 'sweet spot' most owners recommend; NAS D90s came on 265/75R16. 255/85R16 (about 33") is the popular upgrade and generally fits at stock height, but owners report rubbing on the front radius arms at full lock (fix by winding out the steering stops), against the 45 L auxiliary tank on 110s, and close to the spring brackets at full compression on 90s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/defender-90-110/tires/)
- Land Rover Defender (L663), biggest tire: 275/60R20 (about 33 inches) is the popular step up from the factory 255/60R20. A Defender2.net owner fitted it to a coil-sprung truck on stock 8.5-inch 20s with no spacers and reports no rubbing, even off-road; others warn it can touch on some setups. 275/55R20 runs without rubbing on air suspension at full articulation, and Australian owners run 275/65R18 LT on 18s. The OCTA fits 33s from the factory because its axles move forward slightly. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/defender-l663/tires/)
- Land Rover Discovery Series I, best years and years to avoid: Condition first: Disco 1s rot in the sills, floors and rear chassis, so a solid truck of any year beats a shiny rotten one. After that, the 1994-on facelift with the 300Tdi is the one guides point to; Classic Car Hub calls it the more sensible choice and says it commands a premium over the V8. One LandyZone member's tip is a late ES (1997–98 model year), or a 1998 Anniversary for most of the kit without the leaky sunroofs. US trucks were all V8s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-1/years/)
- Land Rover Discovery Series I, biggest tire: Factory sizes were 205R16 and 235/70R16, which are almost the same height. On a stock-height, stock-geared truck, a LandyZone owner recommends going no bigger than 245/75R16 (about 30.5 inches), which several members run. Owners do run 33s and bigger with lifts; one member says 35s want at least a 4.1 and ideally a 4.37 ring and pinion. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-1/tires/)
- Land Rover Discovery Series II, best years and years to avoid: There isn't an agreed best year. Wikipedia notes early Td5s (1998–2000) suffered oil-pump-drive and head-stud failures that were fixed within two years. In the US, an Expedition Portal buying guide says 2003–04 trucks were the worst for cracked oil pumps and more prone to loose liners, and a LandRoverForums thread gives the 2003–04 4.6 the worst reputation, though other owners there still vote for the 2004 for its facelift and diff-lock lever. Whatever the year, buy the one with head-gasket, cooling and chassis receipts. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-2/years/)
- Land Rover Discovery Series II, biggest tire: Discoweb owners recommend 245/75R16 for a stock-height truck. Several run 265/75R16 at stock height, but they rub at full lock on the plastic behind the fog lamps or need the front bumper trimmed. With a 2-inch lift such as the OME kit, 265/75R16 is the common choice; 285/75R16 wants nearer 3 inches and raises gearing and halfshaft-strength concerns. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-2/tires/)
- Land Rover LR3 / Discovery 3, best years and years to avoid: Later is better, within reason. The 2005 LR3 has the most NHTSA complaints (96, against 8 for 2008 and 3 for 2009) and five recalls, and ReRev names 2005 the one to avoid and 2008–09 the most reliable. Raw complaint counts aren't adjusted for how many were sold, though, and PistonHeads still calls any phase-one Discovery 3 a high-risk purchase, so a thick service file beats a late build date. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr3/years/)
- Land Rover LR3 / Discovery 3, biggest tire: On 18-inch wheels, 265/65R18 or 285/60R18 (about 31 in) fit at factory height without modification. 275/65R18 (about 32 in) is about the biggest that works at stock height, and owners report it needs the front-left height-sensor wire zip-tied to the frame rail and a little liner reshaping; one owner's 285/65R18s rubbed slightly at full lock. With lift rods, 275/65R18 is the common choice. One owner advises staying under 32 in overall. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr3/tires/)
- Land Rover LR4 / Discovery 4, best years and years to avoid: There's no clean answer. The 2010–13 V8s are the ones with standard low range, but treat every one as a timing-chain risk until you see the tensioner and lever invoice; the class-action settlement covered 2012–2014 5.0 trucks. The 2014–16 supercharged V6 avoids that problem and ReRev rates those years best, but low range and the rear locker came only with the Heavy Duty package, and the plastic cooling parts fail on both engines. Buy the records, then the year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr4/years/)
- Land Rover LR4 / Discovery 4, biggest tire: US trucks came on 255/50R19 or 255/50R20. On the 20s, LandRoverWorld owners say 265/50R20 fits at standard height without rubbing and is the largest size that still fits the spare well when fully inflated. A 285/50R20 rubs slightly at full lock and needs the spare deflated to fit underneath. Owners who switch to aftermarket 18-inch wheels run 265/65R18 with no rubbing at standard height; 285/60R18 brings only mild liner rub at full compression or lock. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr4/tires/)
- Lexus LX 450, best years and years to avoid: There are only two, and they're nearly the same. The 1996 and 1997 trucks both have the A343F, airbags and OBD-II. Buy the one with the best records, the healthiest knuckles and working lockers. Factory lockers add about $2,500 in value according to forum regulars, so a locked truck is worth the wait. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx450/years/)
- Lexus LX 450, biggest tire: The stock size is 275/70R16. On a stock-height 80 Series or LX 450 with healthy springs, the usual answer is 285/75R16, about 33 in. Owners report it works, with some rubbing possible at full flex or full lock. Anything bigger starts rubbing. Slee's guide notes that 35s are possible with a 2-in Old Man Emu lift, but expect to rub when crawling unless you lower the bump stops. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx450/tires/)
- Lexus LX 470, best years and years to avoid: 2003–2005 is the closest thing to a consensus. An Expedition Portal regular calls 2003–05 'THE years to get', and IH8MUD members single out the 2003-on five-speed automatic and redesigned dash. 2000 added VSC, A-TRAC and an improved front differential, so 2000–02 trucks are a cheaper runner-up. 2006–07 trucks get VVT-i and more power but also an air-injection system one member warns can be costly to fix. 2003–2007 trucks should have had the steering-shaft recall done. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx470/years/)
- Lexus LX 470, biggest tire: The IH8MUD 100 Series FAQ answer is 285/75R16 or 285/65R18, both about 33 in, with no lift. An owner with a stock '99 found 295/75R16 a tight fit that might not clear at full bump and full lock. Stock sizes were 16-in wheels to 2002 and 275/60R18 from 2003. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx470/tires/)
- Lexus LX 570, best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus best year, but there is one to be careful with: 2008–2010 trucks have the most radiator-crack reports (IH8MUD notes the part number changed after 2010), and owners say 2008s had water-pump issues. After that it's taste. 2013–2015 add Multi-Terrain Select and Turn Assist; 2016-on gets the eight-speed and a new interior. ClubLexus owners split on 2015 versus 2016: some find the facelift's tech and radar cruise worth it, others say the 2016 drives worse. There is no 2012 model year in the US. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx570/years/)
- Lexus LX 570, biggest tire: The stock size is 285/50R20. The practical limit is about 33 in, and even that meant moving the front fender liner forward about an inch on one IH8MUD member's LX. His 35x12.5R20 build needed the liner moved further, the sidestep return trimmed and the body mount reshaped, with spacers giving about +35 mm effective offset. The LX is easier to fit than a Land Cruiser because it doesn't have the KDSS bar. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx570/tires/)
- Lexus LX 600, best years and years to avoid: Too new for a consensus. 2022–2024 trucks are the ones with paperwork to check: engine recalls 24V-381 and 25V-767, plus a neutral-rollaway software recall. NHTSA doesn't list those engine recalls for 2025, but 2025–2026 trucks have their own transmission-ECU software recall (26V-094). Whichever year, run the VIN. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx600/years/)
- Lexus LX 600, biggest tire: The factory size on 22s is 265/50R22, about 32 in. Owners on aftermarket 20s run 275/60R20 (about 33 in) and 285/55R20 without rubbing, and 275/70R18 fits on Toyota TRD 18-inch wheels. 285/50R22 on factory wheels needed cutting and spacers. Without a lift, plan on about 33 in. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx600/tires/)
- Lexus GX 470, best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus year. Every GX 470 has the same 2UZ-FE V8 and A750F five-speed automatic; 2005 added VVT-i (270 hp, restated as 263 hp from 2006). Some Expedition Portal members hold out for a VVT-i truck, but the thread's own starter calls it a mixed bag, one ClubLexus owner who drove both says you can't tell the difference to 60 mph, and that thread's starter reckons quality is much the same across the model years. Trucks from mid-2004 get the 6,500 lb hitch and 2008–2009 the facelift. In practice, rust, timing-belt records, air suspension, steering rack and manifold matter more than the build date. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx470/years/)
- Lexus GX 470, biggest tire: The stock size is 265/65R17. On a stock or nearly stock GX 470, the safe consensus is about 31.5 inches. Owners report 265/70R17 working with little or no rubbing (one reports a slight rub at full lock in reverse), and 255/75R17 with zero rubbing. Going to 33 inches (285/70R17, or the narrower 255/80R17) generally means a 2–3 in lift and some liner trimming. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx470/tires/)
- Lexus GX 460, best years and years to avoid: 2014 and later. ClubLexus moderators call air-pump failure common on 2010–2013 trucks and say it should be far less of an issue on 2014-on, though the valves can still fail. 2014-on also gets the spindle-grille facelift; 2020-on Off-Road package trucks add Crawl Control, MTS and a transmission cooler, and 2022–2023 add CarPlay. If you buy a 2010–2013, confirm the updated air-pump parts are in. Lexus changed little mechanically, so condition and records still matter more than year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx460/years/)
- Lexus GX 460, biggest tire: Stock is P265/60R18, about 30.5 in. One owner reports 255/70R18 (about 32.1 in) fitting a stock 460 with no rubbing. 265/70R18 tends to touch plastics at full lock. On 17s, GXOR's database has 275/65R17 on stock suspension with only a slight liner rub at full turn. Treat about 32 in as the no-lift limit. 33s want a lift, and 35s need a 2–2.5 in lift plus UCAs, a body mount chop, liner removal and pinch-weld work. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx460/tires/)
- Lexus GX 550, best years and years to avoid: It's too new for a consensus. The one documented problem year is 2024: recall 25V-767 covers early 2024 trucks for V35A machining debris, so check the VIN and get the dealer paperwork. NHTSA lists that recall for 2024 GXs only; 2025 trucks share the camera-software and load-label recalls but not the engine one. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx550/years/)
- Lexus GX 550, biggest tire: The Overtrail comes on 33-inch all-terrains and 18-inch wheels. On IH8MUD's LC250/GX550 tire thread, 265/70R18 fits with no problems and many owners run 275/70R18 (about 33.2 in) without mods. 285/70R18 is where rubbing starts. 35s generally need a level or small lift. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx550/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz Unimog 404, biggest tire: There's no lift-kit culture here: the portal axles already give about 400 mm (15.7 in) of clearance. Stock is 10.5-20 (275/80R20) on 9.00-20 rims, and the factory also approved 12.5R20 (335/80R20) on 11.00-20 rims in Continental MPT 81 or Michelin XZL. One Steel Soldiers owner runs 12.50 Michelins and says they won't fit the under-bed spare carrier unless you move the battery box. Anything bigger is custom work. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/unimog/unimog-404/tires/)
- Mercedes-Benz Unimog U1300L (435), biggest tire: Most U1300Ls in the US run 20-inch Continental MPT 81s or Michelin XZLs in 335/80R20 (12.5R20, about 40.6 in tall) or 365/80R20 (14.5R20, about 42.9 in), and several BaT trucks wear 365/80R20 MPT 81s. One builder chose 365s with fast axles to keep first gear low enough for trails. A 395/85R20 is too big for a U1300 without a cab lift, according to one Expedition Portal member, and it also loads the portal bearings, which are expensive. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/unimog/unimog-u1300l/tires/)
- Mitsubishi Delica Star Wagon (L300 4WD), biggest tire: About 30 inches. Delica.ca's tech library says 30x9.50R15 tyres fit in most cases without issues, and 235/75R15s are a common fitment on imported vans. The stock size was 215SR15 on 15x6 wheels with a 6 x 139.7 mm bolt pattern. A 7-inch-wide wheel with the stock offset should fit, but an 8-inch wheel may touch the upper ball joint. Anything larger needs a lift and trimming of the seam at the rear of the front wheel arch. Make sure the torsion bars haven't sagged before you blame the tyre. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/delica/delica-l300/tires/)
- Mitsubishi Delica Space Gear, biggest tire: Not much bigger than stock. Japanese 4WD vans came on 225/80R15s, which are about 29 inches, on 15x6 wheels with about 4.25 inches of backspacing. A long-time Delica Canada member says 245/75R16 may fit unlifted, but only with a lot of trimming, and you'll need a lift to clear the wheel wells at full articulation. Even with a 2-inch lift, owners report 31x10.5s rubbing on compression in turns after trimming. One said he should have gone with 30s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/delica/delica-space-gear/tires/)
- Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (First Generation), biggest tire: We couldn't find a clear forum consensus for the first generation. Documented examples include a BaT 1990 Montero LS on 285/70R17 tyres (about 33 inches) on aftermarket 17-inch wheels; the listing doesn't mention a lift. Most first-generation trucks run 15-inch wheels. Measure your clearance at full lock and full stuff before you buy tyres. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen1/tires/)
- Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (Second Generation), best years and years to avoid: There's no buyer consensus on a best year. JDM Buy Sell's guide doesn't name one, and owners argue about engines rather than years. What you can avoid is the NADI driver airbag. NHTSA recall 20V035000 covers 1998–2000 US Monteros, with a free replacement inflator, and Mitsubishi Australia is buying back NL Pajeros built between 31 May 1996 and 30 September 2000 because no replacement inflator exists. Run the VIN before you pay. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen2/years/)
- Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (Second Generation), biggest tire: We found no single forum consensus, but the evidence points to about 31 inches. An Australian owner lists the 1996 NL GLX's stock tyres as 235/75R15 on 15x6 steel wheels and calls 31x10.5R15 'a good tyre size'. BaT's 1994 Montero SR runs 31x10.50R15s on its factory 15-inch alloys, and a 1995 Pajero sold on 265/70R16s. Go bigger and you'll want a lift, and probably some trimming. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen2/tires/)
- Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (Third Generation), biggest tire: About 33 inches if it's narrow. Owners on Expedition Portal run 235/85R16 and 255/85R16 (about 33 in) on stock suspension with no rubbing, and one '05 owner runs LT265/70R17. A 285/75R16 is a step too far: owners report it rubbing at full lock even with an OME lift. A veteran owner's advice is that '265/75R16 or 17 are the best fit on these rigs, even lifted.' Stock tires on BaT's 2001 Limited are 265/70R16. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen3/tires/)
- Nissan Patrol 60 Series, biggest tire: We couldn't find a forum consensus for the 60, so here's what's documented. Stock was a narrow 16-inch bias-ply, 7.00-16 or 7.50x16 depending on the truck. One 1969 on Bring a Trailer runs 30x9.50 tyres on 15-inch wheels. A 1982 Colombian LG-61 runs 33x12.50 tyres on 15s, with longer rear shackles. Narrow tall tyres such as a 7.50x16 suit the truck's look, gearing and steering best. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/patrol-60/tires/)
- Nissan Patrol 160 / MQ, biggest tire: About 31x10.50. In an ExplorOz thread, an owner on stock, saggy springs was running 31x10.5s, and another suggested 32x11.5s might fit once springs were reset. The consensus for 33s is a 2-inch spring lift. For 35s, owners add a 2-inch body lift, and 38s took a 3-inch body lift with longer shackles. MQs don't have much wheel travel, so guard clearance is tight but workable. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/160-mq/tires/)
- Nissan Patrol Y60 (GQ), best years and years to avoid: No particular year. Guides and owners choose a GQ by engine, not by build date. 4X4 Australia says the TD42 was the outback tourers' favourite for its simplicity and 'legendary reliability', and NissanPatrol.com.au members say TD42s fetch a premium over the TB42 petrol and the smaller engines. Wikipedia notes that the RD28T and TB42 suffer head-gasket trouble when driven hard, and Perth dealer Westside Auto calls the RD28T underpowered for towing. Some owners prefer a pre-August-1993 'Silvertop' TD42, because Wikipedia says the lightened engine is weaker, but others say the black-tops are still very strong. Buy the best-kept TD42 manual you can find. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y60/years/)
- Nissan Patrol Y60 (GQ), biggest tire: 4X4 Australia says its 1988 GQ wore 31-inch all-terrains from the factory, and 31x10.50R15 or a similarly sized 16-inch tyre is the safe size on standard suspension. A 33 does fit 'into the GQ wheel arch, but only just', according to the Patrol 4x4 Club SA forum. On NissanPatrol.com.au, owners say 33x12.5s on zero-offset rims scrub the inner guards at full flex. The common recipe is a 2-inch lift with 33x12.5R15s on negative-offset wheels (owners quote -22 to -24 mm), which push the tyres out past the factory flares. Even then, expect some rub at full lock or full flex, often on the front mud-flap bracket. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y60/tires/)
- Nissan Patrol Y61 (GU), best years and years to avoid: For a touring diesel, the TD42 years. CarsGuide calls the TD42 turbo-diesel 'the pick of the Patrol engines from this era', and Westside Auto names the 2005–07 TD42T ST and ST-L as the GU's sweet spot for reliability. The TD42T arrived in 1999 and the intercooled TD42Ti in 2003, and Australian sources date the end of the TD42 to 2006 or 2007. Be wary of 2000–2003 ZD30s. In the Gulf, where petrol GUs dominate, CarSwitch rates the 2008–10 Safaris as the most refined Y61s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y61/years/)
- Nissan Patrol Y61 (GU), biggest tire: 265/75R16 is the popular stock-height size on ExplorOz, and some owners run 285/75R16 (about 33 in) on 16-inch rims. One owner runs 305/70R16 on a 2004 GU with only a 'tiny' scrub at full lock in reverse. Bigger sizes such as 305/70R17 and 35s are generally reported with at least a 2 in lift and the mud flaps removed. Many GUs won't take 15-inch rims over their brakes. In Australia, check your state's current limit on tyre-diameter increases; owners note Nissan sold a replacement tyre placard for 265/75R16. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y61/tires/)
- Nissan Patrol Y62 / Armada, best years and years to avoid: CarSwitch, a UAE used-car marketplace, rates 2015–2017 trucks as the value sweet spot and the 2020–2021 facelifts as the best recent buys. Perth dealer Westside Auto calls the 2020-on facelift Patrols the most desirable on the used market. CarSwitch suggests caution with 2010–2012 trucks because of transmission valve-body problems and early fit-and-finish issues. In the US, run any 2020–2021 Armada's VIN for the fuel-pump recall. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y62/years/)
- Nissan Patrol Y62 / Armada, biggest tire: We couldn't find a solid owner consensus for a stock Y62. Stock is 265/70R18 on Australian Patrols and the Armada SV, or 275/60R20 on higher grades. 6061 Works lists 275/70R18 as a mild upgrade, about 15 mm taller than stock. For 295/70R18, Nissan's own Warrior needed a 29 mm suspension lift, and 6061 Works recommends that size after a 2-inch lift. Nissan sells re-gear sets for trucks on 35s. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y62/tires/)
- Steyr-Puch Pinzgauer 710 / 712, biggest tire: About 33 inches. Portal Hub owners settle on 255/85R16 as the sweet spot, roughly the height of the original Maloyas (which they measure at about 245 mm wide), and 265/75R16 is close to stock size. 285/75R16 goes on but rubs at full lock, and one owner says Discount Tire stopped mounting that size on the narrow factory rims. Another owner's rule: 33s are the maximum 'unless you like wheel well rubbing on the right front side,' and 32s are the smallest worth running. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/pinzgauer/pinzgauer-710-712/tires/)
- Steyr-Puch Pinzgauer 716 / 718, biggest tire: The Turbo D's swing-axle suspension has no lift kits to speak of, so this is about gearing more than clearance. Owners' favorite is 255/85R16, about the same height as a 285/75R16 but narrower, which one Belgian owner says 'just fits perfect'. German Wikipedia says the trucks often run 235/85R16s, and ATL put 285/75R16 BFGoodrich Mud-Terrains on its 2.5 TDI 718. A US owner advises against 285s on a 2.4 because of the extra drag and scrub, and found 34-inch 8.25 tires too tall for the engine. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/pinzgauer/pinzgauer-716-718/tires/)
- Land Rover Range Rover Classic, best years and years to avoid: Buy the most rust-free truck you can afford; condition matters more than the year. Values run from Velar prototypes to two-doors to four-doors, and fuel-injected and LSE four-doors are worth more than carburettor trucks. In the US, choose between 1987–92 coil-sprung SWB trucks and the 1993–95 County LWB with the 4.2 and air suspension. The 1995 trucks get the soft dash. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/classic/years/)
- Land Rover Range Rover Classic, biggest tire: The usual forum answer is 245/75R16 (about 30.5 inches) on stock coils, with the steering stops adjusted to stop rubbing at full lock. Some owners run 265/75R16 with slight chassis rub fixed by the stops. 235/85R16 generally needs a lift or some trimming on these 100-inch trucks. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/classic/tires/)
- Land Rover Range Rover P38A, best years and years to avoid: Hagerty's advice is to buy on condition and specification rather than age, adding that the electrical faults that dogged these trucks are now understood and fixable. ReRev says 1998 drew the most complaints of any Range Rover year on CarComplaints. Mid-1999-on V8s have Bosch Motronic instead of GEMS, but no guide we found says that alone makes them the better buy; cooling-system history matters more. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/p38/years/)
- Land Rover Range Rover P38A, biggest tire: Forum reports say 245/75R16 or 255/70R16, roughly 30 to 30.5 inches. One owner runs 255/70R16 on standard suspension with no rubbing. Another found 245/75R16 clears at full lock at standard and high ride heights, but rubs at the lowest height and can touch the back of the arch at full compression. 265/75R16 (about 31.6 in) rubs when the axles cross up unless you lift the truck and fit an adjustable Panhard rod. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/p38/tires/)
- Land Rover Range Rover L322, best years and years to avoid: Owners and buyers' guides generally rate the 2007–2009 Jaguar-engined trucks best: Terrain Response, a locking centre diff and the six-speed ZF. Buy a 2003–2005 BMW 4.4 only with receipts for timing guides (or if you'll do them yourself). Buy a 2010–2012 5.0 only with evidence that the chain tensioners and guides have been updated. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l322/years/)
- Land Rover Range Rover L322, biggest tire: On 18-inch wheels, owners say 265/60R18 (about 30.5 in) fits with no problems, including off-road. 265/65R18 has been warned against because it can rub when the air suspension drops. On 20s, 275/55R20 clears the bump stops but rubs the liners at full steering lock. Check that a taller spare still fits in the well. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l322/tires/)
- Land Rover Range Rover L405, biggest tire: On 20-inch wheels, the FullFatRR consensus is 285/50R20 (about 31.2 in). Two owners run them, one calls them probably the largest that won't rub in any height mode, and the spare still fits the well. 275/55R20 (about 31.9 in) is also fitted by 'quite a few' owners, though one member predicted it might just catch at full lock. Twenty inches is the smallest rim owners trust to clear the brakes, and 255/60R20 tyres on new-Defender wheels also fit. Want bigger? Lucky8 has a video on trimming the bumper for larger tyres on its lifted Project L405. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l405/tires/)
- Land Rover Range Rover L460, best years and years to avoid: Too early to call. NHTSA lists ten or eleven recalls for each of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 model years, so later trucks aren't clean either: 2022–23 carry the cam-carrier, seat-frame and tail-light campaigns, and 2024 adds panel-bonding, transmission and oil-filter-housing recalls. Owners prefer the 2024-on S68 V8. Buy on a closed recall list, a warranty and software that actually updates, not on the model year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l460/years/)
- Land Rover Range Rover L460, biggest tire: There is no forum consensus yet. Owners haven't published L460 all-terrain fitment the way L405 owners have, and the off-the-shelf sensor-link lift kits sold for the L405 don't list the L460. Factory wheels run from 20 to 23 inches, and one owner fitted L460 21s with 275/50R21 tyres to an L405. If you want sidewall, 20-inch wheels are the realistic floor: Lucky8 lists 20×9.5 ET30 wheels for the L460, and L405 20s fit with the correct flat-seat bolts. Test any oversize tyre at full lock and in every height mode before you trust it. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l460/tires/)
- Suzuki Jimny LJ series, biggest tire: We couldn't find a reliable owner consensus. Suzuki fitted 16-inch wheels to the LJ10 and 15-inch wheels to the LJ20 van. With kei-sized wheel arches and tracks around 1,100–1,200 mm, staying close to the stock size is the safe choice. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/lj-series/tires/)
- Suzuki SJ / Samurai, best years and years to avoid: There's no consensus. MotorTrend says 1986–88 trucks ride more firmly; the '1988½' update brought softer springs, a thicker front anti-roll bar and a 0.865 fifth gear (the 1986 brochure lists 0.795), and 1990–95 trucks have throttle-body injection. On Zukiworld, owners split: some prefer the carbureted 1986–89 trucks because a carb is easy to fix in the field, others the fuel-injected 1990–95 trucks, and one prefers pre-1988½ trucks for their all-metal radiators. Condition and the quality of past modifications matter more than the year. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/samurai/years/)
- Suzuki SJ / Samurai, biggest tire: About a 215/75R15. On Zukiworld, owners say a 215/75R15 fits a stock Samurai with no modifications and 225s fit with a little effort. A 235/75R15 (about 29 inches) needs trimming and flattened inner fender seams, a 1.5–2 inch lift, or both. Stock tires were P205/70R15 according to the 1986 brochure. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/samurai/tires/)
- Suzuki Jimny JB23 / JB43, best years and years to avoid: BigJimny doesn't name a best year, and it rates both petrol engines as robust: the M13A has a timing chain that doesn't need replacing, while the earlier G13B has a cam belt. The ones to be careful with are the early K9K 700 diesels (2003 to about 2006), which it calls statistically very troublesome, and petrols from about 2005–2008 with the early R72 gearbox, whose bearings can fail (about £700 to fix). Late trucks from about 2014 add low-range traction control. Otherwise, rust decides it. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/jimny-jb23/years/)
- Suzuki Jimny JB23 / JB43, biggest tire: Stock on the Wide/Sierra is 205/70R15 (about 27.1 inches). BigJimny's consensus is that 215/75R15 (about 27.7 inches) is the largest that fits an unmodified truck. 235/75R15 (about 28.8 inches) wants a 2-inch lift, and forum regulars say gen 3s still need some trimming even then, though a few owners run them with minor rubbing at full flex. Anything bigger than 215 really calls for regearing, or you'll cook the clutch or the automatic's fluid. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/jimny-jb23/tires/)
- Suzuki Jimny JB74 / JB64, biggest tire: Stock is 195/80R15. The BigJimny consensus is that 215/75R15 is the biggest that suits the stock rims, though it's only slightly taller. Some Australian owners squeeze 235/75R15s on, but those exceed the stock rims' recommended limits. With a 2-inch lift, 235/75R15s fit with a little trimming of the front bumper. Go bigger and you'll want lower gearing. (https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/jimny-jb74/tires/)
